<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
(\ref{x8}, \ref{x10})
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory whose Hom-categories are all idempotent complete. The Cauchy completion of $\mathbb{B}$, as a category weakly enriched in idempotent complete categories, and the bicategorical idempotent completion of $\mathbb{B}$ are equivalent. It follows, that $\mathbb{B}$ is complete under absolute weighted colimits if and only if it is complete under splittings of 2-idempotents.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
{(Idempotent Complete Category)}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category. An \textit{idempotent} is an endomorphism $p:A\to A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that $p^2=p$.

An idempotent $p$ \textit{splits} if there exists an object $B$, and morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that $f\circ g=\textup{id}_B$ and $g\circ f=p$. The data of $B$, $f$ and $g$ defines a \textit{splitting} of $p$ and we call $B$ a retract of $A$.

A category $\mathcal{C}$ is \textit{idempotent complete} if every idempotent in it splits.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
{(Free Walking Idempotent (Splitting))}
We define $\spadesuit_1$ to be the category with two objects $X$ and $Y$ and morphisms generated by $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$ subject to the relation $f\circ g=\textup{id}_Y$. We call this category the \textit{free walking idempotent splitting}, as functors $F:\spadesuit_1\to\mathcal{C}$ directly correspond to split idempotents in $\mathcal{C}$. Analogously, we define $\clubsuit_1\subseteq\spadesuit_1$ to be the full subcategory on $X$ and call it the \textit{free walking idempotent}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
For a given idempotent $F:\clubsuit_1\to\mathcal{C}$, a splitting corresponds to an extension of $F$ along $\iota:\clubsuit_1\to\spadesuit_1$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{spliscol}
Let $F:\clubsuit_1\to\mathcal{C}$ be an idempotent and denote $F(g\circ f)$ by $p$. The  colimit of $F$ defines a splitting of $p$. This colimit is given by the coequaliser of
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
FX \arrow[r, "\textup{id}_{FX}", shift left=1] \arrow[r, "p"', shift right=1] & FX.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
Furthermore every splitting of $p$ defines such a colimit.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
A splitting of an idempotent is unique up to unique isomorphism.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
{(Idempotent Completion)}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category. We define the \textit{idempotent completion} or \textit{Karoubi envelope} $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ to be the category with the following data.
\begin{itemize}
	\item Objects in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ are idempotents in $\mathcal{C}$, i.e., an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ consists of an object $A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ and a morphism $p:A\to A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that $p^2=p$. We will denote this object by $A_p$ and we will denote $A_{\textup{id}_A}$ simply by $A_{\textup{id}}$.
	\item A 1-morphism between $A_p$ and $B_q$ is given by a morphism $f:A\to B$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that $f\circ p=f$ and $q\circ f=f$.
	\item Composition of morphisms in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ is given by the composition in $\mathcal{C}$.
	\item The identity morphism on $A_p$ is given by $p:A_p\to A_p$. 
\end{itemize}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{kar1com}
For any category $\mathcal{C}$, the idempotent completion $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ is idempotent complete.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $A_p$ be an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ and $e:A_p \to A_p$ an idempotent on $A_p$, i.e., $e\circ p=e$, $p\circ e=e$ and $e^2=e$. It therefore follows that $A_e$ is an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ and we have morphisms $e:A_p\to A_e$ and $e:A_e\to A_p$. Composing these morphisms, we see that $e\circ e=e:A_p\to A_p$ and $e\circ e=e=\textup{id}_{A_e}:A_e\to A_e$. Thus the idempotent $e:A_p\to A_p$ splits.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{eobsplit}
For an object $A_p$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$, $A_p$ is a splitting of the idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{kar1emb}
For every category $\mathcal{C}$, there exists a fully faithful functor $\iota_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$. If $\mathcal{C}$ is furthermore idempotent complete, i.e., every idempotent in $\mathcal{C}$ splits, this functor is an equivalence.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
We define $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ to map an object $A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ onto the object $A_{\textup{id}}$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ and a morphism $f:A\to B$ onto $f:A_{\textup{id}}\to B_{\textup{id}}$. Since any morphism $f:A\to B$ has the property that $f\circ \textup{id}_A=f$ and $\textup{id}_B\circ f=f$, we see that $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ is fully faithful.

Now assume that $\mathcal{C}$ is idempotent complete and let $A_p$ be an object in $\mathcal{C}$. We know that the idempotent $p:A\to A$ splits in $\mathcal{C}$ via an object $B$. We now have $A_p\,\cong\, B_{\textup{id}}$ since they both define splittings of $p:A_{\textup{id}}\to A_{\textup{id}}$ and thus $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ is an equivalence of categories.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{1adj}
Idempotent completion defines a 2-functor $\textup{Kar}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ which is left adjoint to the forgetful 2-functor $\mathcal{U}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The 2-functor $\textup{Kar}$ maps a category $\mathcal{C}$ to the category $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$. A functor $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ is mapped onto the functor $\textup{Kar}(F):\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{D})$ which maps an idempotent $A_p$ onto the idempotent $FA_{Fp}$ and a morphism $f:A_p\to B_q$ onto the morphism $Ff:FA_{Fp}\to FB_{Fq}$. The functoriality of $\textup{Kar}(F)$ follows directly from the functoriality of $F$. Lastly, a natural transformation $\varphi:F\to G$ is mapped onto the natural transformation $\textup{Kar}(\varphi):\textup{Kar}(F)\to\textup{Kar}(G)$ which has components $\textup{Kar}(\varphi)_{A_p}=G(p)\circ\varphi_A=\varphi_A\circ F(p):FA_{Fp}\to GA_{Gp}$. This defines the 2-functor $\textup{Kar}$.

To have an adjunction $\textup{Kar}\vdash\mathcal{U}$, we now need strong transformations $\eta:\textup{id}_\textbf{\textup{Cat}}\to \mathcal{U}\circ\textup{Kar}$ and $\epsilon: \textup{Kar}\circ\mathcal{U}\to \textup{id}_{\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}}$. These will have component 1-morphisms, i.e., functors $\eta_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ and $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}:\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{D})\to \mathcal{D}$ for categories $\mathcal{C}$ and idempotent complete categories $\mathcal{D}$.

Since we already defined functors $\iota_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$, we define $\eta$ to have component 1-morphisms $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ and denote the strong transformation itself simply by $\iota$. This forms a 2-natural transformation as its component 2-morphisms are given by identites. We can define $\epsilon$ and its component 1-morphisms $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}:\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{D})\to\mathcal{D}$ in the following way:

Let $A_p$ be an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{D})$. Since $\mathcal{D}$ is idempotent complete, we have a splitting $(A,B,f,g)$ of $p$, i.e., an object $B$ in $\mathcal{D}$ and morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ such that $g\circ f=p$ and $f\circ g=\textup{id}_B$. To define $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}$, we need to choose a splitting for each idempotent $A_p$ and we choose these such that any identity idempotent $A_{\textup{id}}$ splits via $(A,A,\textup{id}_A,\textup{id}_A)$. We now map the idempotent $A_p$ onto $B$. A morphism $h$ between objects $A_p$ and $A^\prime_{p^\prime}$ that have splittings $(A,B,f,g)$ and $(A^\prime,B^\prime,f^\prime,g^\prime)$ is mapped onto the morphism $f^\prime\circ h\circ g:B\to B^\prime$. One can check that this assignment is functorial.

In general, $\epsilon$ has non-identity component 2-morphisms. For an object $A_p$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{D})$ with a splitting $(A,B,f,g)$ and a functor $F:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{D}^\prime$, the splitting we choose for $FA_{Fp}$ does not have to agree with $(FA,FB,Ff,Fg)$. Still, these splittings must be uniquely isomorphic and we definte $\epsilon$ to have component 2-morphisms given by these unique isomorphisms.

Lastly, we need to check that the two triangle identities $(\epsilon\circ\textup{Kar})\cdot(\textup{Kar}\circ\iota)\,\cong\,\textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}}$ and ${(\mathcal{U}\circ\epsilon)\cdot(\iota\circ\mathcal{U})}\,\cong\,\textup{id}_\mathcal{U}$ hold. By looking at their components, we see that these identities translate to $\epsilon_{\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})}\iota_{\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})}\,\cong\,\textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})}$ and $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}\iota_\mathcal{D}\,\cong\,\textup{id}_\mathcal{D}$, which means we just have to check that $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}\iota_\mathcal{D}\,\cong\,\textup{id}_\mathcal{D}$ holds for any idempotent complete category $\mathcal{D}$. Since we defined $\epsilon_\mathcal{D}$ by choosing that an identity idempotent splits via the identity, this holds automatically.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{kar1equ}
For each category $\mathcal{C}$ and idempotent complete category $\mathcal{D}$, we have an equivalence of categories $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{D})\simeq\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})$ induced by precomposing with $\iota_\mathcal{C}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This follows from the bicategorical generalisation that adjunction induce isomorphisms between Hom-sets and is detailed in proposition \ref{2adjequiv}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
{(Absolute Colimit)}
Let $\mathcal{J}$, $\mathcal{C}$ be categories and $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ a functor. A colimit of $F$ is called an \textit{absolute colimit} if for every category $\mathcal{D}$ and functor $G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$, it is preserved by $G$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
The splitting of an idempotent defines an absolute colimit.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
{(Absolute Functor)}
A functor $V:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{J}$ is called an \textit{absolute functor} if for every category $\mathcal{C}$ and functor $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$, the colimit of $FV:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{C}$ is absolute if it exists.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
We have already seen that $\textup{id}_{\clubsuit_1}:\clubsuit_1\to\clubsuit_1$ defines an absolute functor since the colimit of a functor out of $\clubsuit_1$ is given by the splitting of an idempotent. Another, yet trivial, example is the identity functor $\textup{id}_\mathbbm{1}$ on the terminal category $\mathbbm{1}$ which has one object and no non-trivial morphisms.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
{(Completeness under Absolute Colimits)}
A category $\mathcal{C}$ is called \textit{complete under absolute colimits} if for every absolute functor $V:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{J}$ and every functor $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ the colimit of $FV$ exists.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
{(Cauchy Completion)}
We call an object $A$ in a cocomplete category $\mathcal{C}$ \textit{atomic} if the functor $\mathcal{C}(A,-):\mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ is cocontinuous, i.e., preserves all colimits.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category. The \textit{Cauchy completion} of $\mathcal{C}$ is defined to be the the full subcategory of atomic objects in the category $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})$ of presheaves on $\mathcal{C}$, i.e., an object in this category is a functor $S:\mathcal{C}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ such that $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,-):\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ is cocontinuous. We will denote this category as $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{repato}
Representable presheaves are atomic.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For a given representable presheaf $\mathcal{C}(-,c)$, the functor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(\mathcal{C}(-,c),-):\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ is isomorphic to the functor $\textup{ev}_c:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ given by evaluation at $c$ via the Yoneda lemma. Since colimits in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})$ are computed pointwise, evaluation preserves them, and $\mathcal{C}(-,c)$ is atomic. This also follows from proposition \ref{repato2}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
{(Weighted Colimit)}
Let $\mathcal{J}$, $\mathcal{C}$ be categories, and $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$, $W:\mathcal{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ functors. We call $W$ a \textit{weight}. The colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ is an object representing the functor
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{J})(W,\mathcal{C}(F,-)): \mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}},
\end{align*}
i.e., an object $\textup{colim}^W F$ in $\mathcal{C}$ together with a natural isomorphism 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{C}(\textup{colim}^W F,-)\,\cong\,\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{J})(W,\mathcal{C}(F,-)).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Given a functor $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$, and a weight $W:\mathcal{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ the weighted colimit $\textup{colim}^W F$ can be computed as an ordinary colimit in the following way. Applying the Grothendieck construction to $W$, yields its category of elements $\textup{\raisebox{1pt}\textesh} W$ together with a forgetful functor $\mathcal{U}:\textup{\raisebox{1pt}\textesh} W \to \mathcal{J}$. The colimit of $F \mathcal{U}$ then is canonically isomorphic to the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$. Conversely, every ordinary colimit can be thought of as a weighted colimit by taking the weight to be the functor which maps each object to the set with one element.

This immediately implies that any functor which preserves all ordinary colimits also preserves all weighted colimits and vice versa. This means we do not need to differentiate between different notions of cocontinuity or atomicity.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
{(Absolute Weighted Colimit)}
We call a weighted colimit \textit{absolute} if every functor preserves it. For brevity's sake, we will shorten "absolute weighted colimit" to AWC whenever appropriate. We call a weight $W:\mathcal{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ \textit{absolute} if every colimit weighted by $W$ is an AWC.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Applying the Grothendieck construction to an absolute weight $W:\mathcal{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ yields an absolute functor $\mathcal{U}:\textup{\raisebox{1pt}\textesh} W \to \mathcal{J}$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
{(Completeness under AWCs)}
A category $\mathcal{C}$ is called \textit{complete under AWCs} if for every absolute weight $\mathcal{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ and every functor $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ exists.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{cau1com}
For any category $\mathcal{C}$, its Cauchy completion $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$ is complete under AWCs.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Follows from proposition \ref{cau2com}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{cau1emb}
For every category $\mathcal{C}$, the Yoneda embedding $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})$ takes values in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$ and thus defines a fully faithful functor $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$. If $\mathcal{C}$ is furthermore complete under AWCs, this functor is an equivalence.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Follows from proposition \ref{cau2emb}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{cau1equ}
For any two categories $\mathcal{C}$, $\mathcal{D}$, with $\mathcal{D}$ being complete under AWCs, there is an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}) \,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{D})
\end{align*}
given by precomposition with $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathcal{C}}$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Follows from corollary \ref{cau2equ}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{cau1adj}
Analogously to corollary \ref{kar1equ}, the above equivalence is derived from a left adjoint 2-functor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_{\textup{awc}}$, where $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_{\textup{awc}}$ is the 2-category of categories complete under AWCs. A proof of this statement will be given later.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{ret1ato}
A retract of an atomic object is atomic.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $B$ be a retract of an atomic object $A$ in a category $\mathcal{C}$, i.e., we have morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$ such that $fg=\textup{id}_B$. Let $F:\mathcal{J}\to \mathcal{C}$ be a functor with universal cone $\lambda:F\to\Delta_{\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F}$. We will need to show that $\lambda_*:\mathcal{C}(B,F)\to\Delta_{\mathcal{C}(B,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)}$ also defines a universal cone.

Let $\varphi:\mathcal{C}(B,F)\to \Delta_X$ be a natural transformation, we need to show that there is a unique $\psi:\mathcal{C}(B,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)\to X$ such that the diagram 
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\mathcal{C}(B,F)} \arrow[d, "\lambda_*"] \arrow[r, "\varphi"] & \Delta_X \\
{\Delta_{\mathcal{C}(B,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F})} \arrow[ru, "\psi"']            &         
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
commutes. We can expand this diagram in the following way.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\mathcal{C}(A,F)} \arrow[d, "\lambda_*"] \arrow[r, "g^*", bend left=15] & {\mathcal{C}(B,F)} \arrow[r, "\varphi"] \arrow[d, "\lambda_*"] \arrow[l, "f^*"', bend left=15] & \Delta_X \\
{\Delta_{\mathcal{C}(A,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)}} \arrow[r, "g^*"', bend left=15]               & { \Delta_{\mathcal{C}(B,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)}} \arrow[ru, "\psi"'] \arrow[l, "f^*", bend left=15]            &  
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
Since $A$ is atomic, we know that $\lambda_*:\mathcal{C}(A,F)\to\Delta_{\mathcal{C}(A,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)}$ is a universal cone. We can now define $\widetilde{\varphi}=\varphi \circ g^*$ and thus have a unique $\widetilde{\psi}: \mathcal{C}(A,\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} F)\to X$ such that $\widetilde{\psi}\circ \lambda_*=\widetilde{\varphi}$. We now have a unique $\psi=\widetilde{\psi}\circ f^*$ such that $\psi\circ\lambda_*=\varphi$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{ato1ret}
Every atomic presheaf is a retract of a representable presheaf.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $S$ be an atomic presheaf on $\mathcal{C}$. The density theorem states that each presheaf is a colimit of representables. This means there exists a category $\mathcal{J}$, a functor $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ and a universal cone $\lambda:\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F\to \Delta_S$.

Since $S$ is atomic, applying $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,-)$ yields another universal cone
\begin{align*}
\lambda_*:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F)\to\Delta_{\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,S)}.
\end{align*}
Since the functor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F):\mathcal{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ takes values in $\textbf{\textup{Set}}$, we can explicitly construct a second colimit cone. We define a relation on the set
\begin{align*}
\coprod_{j\in\textup{Ob}\mathcal{J}}\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\mathcal{C}(-,Fj))
\end{align*}
in the following way: For each $\alpha:S\to\mathcal{C}(-,Fj_1)$ and $\beta:S\to\mathcal{C}(-,Fj_2)$, we set $\alpha \sim\beta$ if there exists a morphism $f:j_1\to j_2$ in $\mathcal{J}$ such that $F(f)_*\circ \alpha=\beta$. We now take the equivalence relation generated by this relation and define $\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F)$ to be the set of equivalence classes under this relation. The cone 
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\lambda}:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F)\to\Delta_{\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F)}
\end{align*}
is now defined via $\widetilde{\lambda}_j(\alpha)=[\alpha]$, i.e., for each $j$ in $\mathcal{J}$, $\widetilde{\lambda}_j$ maps $\alpha:S\to \mathcal{C}(-,F(j))$ onto its equivalence class $[\alpha]$. We now also have a unique map
\begin{align*}
\varphi:\textup{colim}_{\mathcal{J}} \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathcal{C} F)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})(S,S)
\end{align*}
such that $\varphi\circ\widetilde{\lambda}=\lambda_*$, which is defined via $\varphi([\alpha])=\lambda_j\circ \alpha$.

We know that this map has to be an isomorphism, which implies that there exists a $j$ in $\mathcal{J}$ and an $\alpha:S\to \mathcal{C}(-,Fj)$ such that $\lambda_j\circ \alpha=\textup{id}_S$. Therefore $\alpha\circ \lambda_j$ is an idempotent on $\mathcal{C}(-,Fj)$, which splits via $S$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{kar1cau}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category. The functor given by the composition
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}) \arrow[r, "\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})}"] & \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})) \arrow[r, "\iota_\mathcal{C}^*"] & \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
defines an equivalence of categories $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})\,\simeq\,\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
First, we want to show that the functor takes values in atomic objects, i.e., for every object $A_p$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$, the presheaf $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_p):\mathcal{C}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ is atomic. By remark \ref{eobsplit}, $A_p$ is a splitting of the idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}$. By absoluteness of splittings, we have that $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_p)$ is a retract of $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_{\textup{id}})=\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},\iota_\mathcal{C} A)$. Since $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ is  fully faithful, we have $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},\iota_\mathcal{C} A)\cong \mathcal{C}(-,A)$. This means that $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_p)$ is a retract of a representable presheaf and by lemma \ref{ret1ato}, it therefore has to be atomic.

Next, we will show that the functor is fully faithful. Since the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful and by corollary \ref{kar1equ} with $\mathcal{D}=\textbf{\textup{Set}}^\textup{op}$, precomposition with $\iota_\mathcal{C}$ is fully faithful, their composition must also be fully faithful.

Lastly, we need to show that the functor is essentially surjective. Let $S$ be an atomic presheaf on $\mathcal{C}$. By proposition \ref{ato1ret}, there exists an object $A$ in $\mathcal{C}$ and an idempotent $p$ on $A$ such that $S$ is a splitting of the idempotent $p_*$ on $\mathcal{C}(-,A)$. By remark \ref{eobsplit}, $A_p$ is a splitting of the idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}=\iota_\mathcal{C} A$. By absoluteness of splittings, $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_p)$ is a splitting of the idempotent $p_*$ on $\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},\iota_\mathcal{C} A)\,\cong\,\mathcal{C}(-,A)$. Since splittings of idempotents are unique up to isomorphisms, it follows that $S\,\cong\, \textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})(\iota_\mathcal{C},A_p)$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
The 2-functor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_{\textup{awc}}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor $\mathcal{U}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_{\textup{awc}}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Combining theorem \ref{1adj} with theorem \ref{kar1cau} yields the desired result.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{icisabc}
A category is idempotent complete if and only if it is complete under AWCs.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an idempotent complete category. By proposition \ref{kar1emb} and theorem \ref{kar1cau}, we now have $\mathcal{C}\,\simeq\,\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$. Since $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathcal{C})$ is complete under AWCs, $\mathcal{C}$ also must be. The opposite direction follows analogously with proposition \ref{cau1emb}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{abssplit}
Every absolute colimit is a retract of an object in the image of its defining functor.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $F:\mathcal{J}\to\mathcal{C}$ be a functor and let $\lambda:F\to \Delta_A$ define an absolute colimit for some $A$ in $\mathcal{C}$. We want to show that $A$ is a retract of an object in the image of $F$. If we apply the functor $\mathcal{C}(A,-):\mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$ to the given colimit, we get a universal cone $\lambda_*:\mathcal{C}(A,F)\to \Delta_{\mathcal{C}(A,A)}$. Since $\mathcal{C}(A,F)$ is now a functor into $\textbf{\textup{Set}}$, there is, analogously to the proof of proposition \ref{ato1ret}, an idempotent $p:Fj\to Fj$ for a $j$ in $\mathcal{J}$ which splits via $A$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
Furthermore, we conjecture that this idempotent $p:Fj\to Fj$ lies in the image of $F$ as well.
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
{(2-Idempotent)}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory. A \textit{2-idempotent} in $\mathbb{B}$ consists of an object $A$ in $\mathbb{B}$, a 1-morphism $p:A\to A$ and 2-morphisms $m:p^2\to p$ and $\Delta:p\to p^2$ such that 
	\begin{align*}
	(\textup{id}_p\circ m)\cdot(\Delta\circ \textup{id}_p) & =(m\circ \textup{id}_p)\cdot(\textup{id}_p\circ\Delta)=\Delta\cdot m \text{ and}\\ 
	m\cdot \Delta & =\textup{id}_p.
	\end{align*}
We denote a 2-idempotent by $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ and whenever it is clear from context, we will simply denote it as $A_p$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
{(2-Idempotent Splitting)}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory and let $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ be a 2-idempotent in $\mathbb{B}$. A \textit{splitting} of $A_p$ is given by an object $B$ in $\mathbb{B}$, 1-morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$, 2-morphisms $\varphi:f\circ g\to \textup{id}_B$, $\psi:\textup{id}_B \to f\circ g$ and an isomorphism $\gamma:g\circ f\to p$ such that $m=\gamma\cdot(\textup{id}_g \circ \varphi \circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot(\gamma^{-1}\circ\gamma^{-1})$ and $\Delta=(\gamma\circ\gamma)\cdot(\textup{id}_g \circ \psi \circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot\gamma^{-1}$. We say that the 2-idempotent $p$ \textit{splits} and we call $B$ a \textit{2-retract} of $A$. We will later show that in certain cases a splitting of a 2-idempotent is unique up to equivalence.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
{(2-Idempotent Completeness)}
We call a bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ \textit{2-idem\-po\-tent complete} if it is locally idempotent complete and if every 2-idempotent in $\mathbb{B}$ splits.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
{(Free Walking 2-Idempotent (Splitting))} \label{walkin}
We will define the bicategory $\spadesuit_2$ to be the bicategory with two objects $X$ and $Y$, 1-morphisms freely generated by $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$ and 2-morphisms freely generated by $\varphi:f\circ g\to \textup{id}_Y$ and $\psi:\textup{id}_Y \to f\circ g$ satisfying the relation $\varphi\cdot\psi=\textup{id}_{\textup{id}_Y}$. We will call this bicategory $\spadesuit_2$ the \textit{free walking 2-idempotent splitting}.

The bicategory $\clubsuit_2$ is defined to be the full subbicategory of $\spadesuit_2$ on the object $X$. We will call this bicategory the \textit{free walking 2-idempotent} and we have a fully faithful pseudofunctor $\iota:\clubsuit_2\to\spadesuit_2$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{ExtIsSplit}
We can now also think of a 2-idempotent in $\mathbb{B}$ as a pseudofunctor $F:\clubsuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$ since every such pseudofunctor determines a 2-idempotent and we can define such a pseudofunctor simply by choosing a 2-idempotent in $\mathbb{B}$. Furthermore, a splitting of $F$ is then given by a functor $F^\prime:\spadesuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$ such that $F^\prime\iota\,\simeq\, F$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
{(Idempotent Completion)}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally idempotent complete bicategory. We define the \textit{idempotent completion} $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ to have the following data:

\begin{itemize}
	\item Objects in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ are 2-idempotents in $\mathbb{B}$, i.e., an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is a collection $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ consisting of an object $A$ in $\mathbb{B}$, a 1-morphism $p:A\to A$ in $\mathbb{B}$ and 2-morphisms $m:p^2\to p$ and $\Delta:p\to p^2$ in $\mathbb{B}$ such that
	\begin{align*}
	(\textup{id}_p\circ m)\cdot(\Delta\circ \textup{id}_p) & =(m\circ \textup{id}_p)\cdot(\textup{id}_p\circ\Delta)=\Delta\cdot m \text{ and}\\ 
	m\cdot \Delta & =\textup{id}_p.
	\end{align*}
	Graphically, this can be represented as follows:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tikzpicture}
	\draw[dashed] (0,6) --(2,6) --(2,8) --(0,8) --(0,6);
	\draw[dashed] (3,6) --(5,6) --(5,8) --(3,8) --(3,6);
	\draw[dashed] (6,6) --(8,6) --(8,8) --(6,8) --(6,6);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (1,6) to (1,8);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (3.75,6) to (3.75,6.75) to[out=90,in=180] (4,7) to[out=0,in=90] (4.25,6.75) to (4.25,6);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (4,7) to (4,8);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (7,6) to (7,7);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (6.75,8) to (6.75,7.25) to[out=270,in=180] (7,7) to[out=0,in=270] (7.25,7.25) to (7.25,8);
	\node[right] at (0,7) {$A$};
	\node[left] at (2,7) {$A$};
	\node[right] at (1,7.5) {$p$};
	\node at (1,5.6) {$\textup{id}_p$};
	\node at (4,5.6) {$m$};
	\node at (7,5.6) {$\Delta$}; 

	\draw[dashed] (0,3) --(2,3) --(2,5) --(0,5) --(0,3);
	\draw[dashed] (3,3) --(5,3) --(5,5) --(3,5) --(3,3);
	\draw[dashed] (6,3) --(8,3) --(8,5) --(6,5) --(6,3);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.5,5) to (0.5,3.75) to[out=270,in=180] (0.75,3.5) to[out=0,in=270] (1,3.75) to (1,4.25) to[out=90,in=180] (1.25,4.5) to[out=0,in=90] (1.5,4.25) to (1.5,3);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.75,3) to (0.75,3.5);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (1.25,4.5) to (1.25,5);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (3.5,3) to (3.5,4.25) to[out=90,in=180] (3.75,4.5) to[out=0,in=90] (4,4.25) to (4,3.75) to[out=270,in=180] (4.25,3.5) to[out=0,in=270] (4.5,3.75) to (4.5,5);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (3.75,5) to (3.75,4.5);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (4.25,3.5) to (4.25,3);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (6.75,3) to (6.75,3.5) to[out=90,in=180] (7,3.75) to[out=0,in=90] (7.25,3.5) to (7.25,3);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (6.75,5) to (6.75,4.5) to[out=270,in=180] (7,4.25) to[out=0,in=270] (7.25,4.5) to (7.25,5);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (7,3.75) to (7,4.25);
	\node at (2.5,4) {$=$};
	\node at (5.5,4) {$=$};
	\node at (3.25,2.6) {$(\textup{id}_p\circ m)\cdot(\Delta\circ\textup{id}_p)=(m\circ\textup{id}_p)\cdot(\textup{id}_p\circ\Delta)=\Delta\cdot m$};

	\draw[dashed] (1.5,0) --(3.5,0) --(3.5,2) --(1.5,2) --(1.5,0);
	\draw[dashed] (4.5,0) --(6.5,0) --(6.5,2) --(4.5,2) --(4.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (2.75,1) to[out=90,in=0] (2.5,1.25) to[out=180,in=90] (2.25,1) to[out=270,in=180] (2.5,0.75) to[out=0,in=270] (2.75,1);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (2.5,0) to (2.5,0.75);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (2.5,1.25) to (2.5,2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (5.5,0) to (5.5,2);
	\node at (4,1) {$=$};
	\node at (2.5,-0.4) {$m\cdot\Delta$};
	\node at (4,-0.4) {$=$};
	\node at (5.5,-0.4) {$\textup{id}_p$};
	\end{tikzpicture}
	\end{center}
	With these identities, we can derive the following equation:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tikzpicture}
	\draw[dashed] (0,0) --(2,0) --(2,2) --(0,2) --(0,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.5,0) to (0.5,0.75) to[out=90,in=180] (0.75,1) to[out=0,in=90] (1,0.75) to (1,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.75,1) to[out=90,in=180] (1.125,1.375) to[out=0,in=90] (1.5,1) to (1.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (1.125,1.375) to (1.125,2);
	\draw[dashed] (4,0) --(6,0) --(6,2) --(4,2) --(4,0);
    \draw[line width=0.35mm] (4.5,0) to (4.5,0.83) to[out=90,in=180] (4.67,1) to[out=0,in=90] (4.83,0.83) to[out=270,in=180] (5,0.66) to[out=0,in=270] (5.17,0.83) to[out=90,in=180] (5.33,1) to[out=0,in=90] (5.5,0.83) to (5.5,0);
    \draw[line width=0.35mm] (5,0) to (5,0.66);
    \draw[line width=0.35mm] (4.67,1) to[out=90,in=180] (5,1.33) to[out=0,in=90] (5.33,1);
    \draw[line width=0.35mm] (5,1.33) to (5,2);
	\node at (3,1) {$=$};
	\node at (3.6,-0.4) {$m\cdot(m\circ\textup{id}_p)\quad =\ m\cdot(m\circ m)\cdot(\textup{id}_p\circ\Delta\circ\textup{id}_p)$};
	\end{tikzpicture}
	\end{center}
From this, we can derive associativity and analogously coassociativity.
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tikzpicture}
	\draw[dashed] (0,0) --(2,0) --(2,2) --(0,2) --(0,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.5,0) to (0.5,0.75) to[out=90,in=180] (0.75,1) to[out=0,in=90] (1,0.75) to (1,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (0.75,1) to[out=90,in=180] (1.125,1.375) to[out=0,in=90] (1.5,1) to (1.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (1.125,1.375) to (1.125,2);
	\draw[dashed] (3,0) --(5,0) --(5,2) --(3,2) --(3,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (4.5,0) to (4.5,0.75) to[out=90,in=0] (4.25,1) to[out=180,in=90] (4,0.75) to (4,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (4.25,1) to[out=90,in=0] (3.875,1.375) to[out=180,in=90] (3.5,1) to (3.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (3.875,1.375) to (3.875,2);
	
	\draw[dashed] (6.5,0) --(8.5,0) --(8.5,2) --(6.5,2) --(6.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (7,2) to (7,1.25) to[out=270,in=180] (7.25,1) to[out=0,in=270] (7.5,1.25) to (7.5,2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (7.25,1) to[out=270,in=180] (7.625,0.625) to[out=0,in=270] (8,1) to (8,2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (7.625,0.625) to (7.625,0);
	\draw[dashed] (9.5,0) --(11.5,0) --(11.5,2) --(9.5,2) --(9.5,0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (11,2) to (11,1.25) to[out=270,in=0] (10.75,1) to[out=180,in=270] (10.5,1.25) to (10.5,2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (10.75,1) to[out=270,in=0] (10.375,0.625) to[out=180,in=270] (10,1) to (10,2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (10.375,0.625) to (10.375,0);
	
	\node at (2.5,1) {$=$};
	\node at (9,1) {$=$};
	\node at (2.5,-0.4) {$m\cdot(m\circ\textup{id}_p)\quad =\quad m\cdot(\textup{id}_p\circ m)$};
	\node at (9,-0.4) {$(\Delta\circ \textup{id}_p)\cdot \Delta\quad =\quad (\textup{id}_p\circ\Delta)\cdot\Delta$};
	\end{tikzpicture}
	\end{center}
	With this, the data $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ forms a special non-unital non-counital Frobenius algebra. Whenever it is clear from context, we will denote $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ as $A_p$ and $A_{\textup{id}_A}$ simply as $A_{\textup{id}}$.  
	\item For each pair of objects $A_p=(A,p,m_p,\Delta_p)$ and $B_q=(B,q,m_q,\Delta_q)$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$, we have a Hom-category $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,B_q)$. A 1-morphism in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is a collection ${(f,\vartriangleleft,\rho,\vartriangleright,\lambda)}$ consisting of a 1-morphism $f:A\to B$ in $\mathbb{B}$ , and 2-morphisms $\vartriangleleft:f\circ p \to f$, $\rho:f\to f\circ p$, $\vartriangleright:q\circ f \to f$ and $\lambda: f\to q\circ f$ in $\mathbb{B}$ such that
	\begin{align*}
	& (\textup{id}_f\circ m_p)\cdot(\rho\circ \textup{id}_p) =(\vartriangleleft\circ \textup{id}_p)\cdot(\textup{id}_f\circ\Delta_p)=\rho\cdot \vartriangleleft, \ \vartriangleleft\cdot \rho=\textup{id}_f, \\
	& (\textup{id}_q\circ \vartriangleright)\cdot(\Delta_q\circ \textup{id}_f) =(m_q\circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot (\textup{id}_q\circ\lambda)=\lambda\cdot \vartriangleright, \ \vartriangleright\cdot \lambda=\textup{id}_f, \\
	& \vartriangleright\cdot(\textup{id}_q\circ\vartriangleleft) =\vartriangleleft\cdot(\vartriangleright\circ\textup{id}_p) \text{ and } (\lambda\circ\textup{id}_p)\cdot\rho=(\textup{id}_q\circ\rho)\cdot\lambda.
	\end{align*}		
	Whenever it is clear from context, we will denote $(f,\vartriangleleft,\rho,\vartriangleright,\lambda)$ as $f:A_p\to B_q$ or even just as $f$. Graphically, this can be represented as follows:
	\tikzmath{\x1 = 0; \y1 =0; 
			\x2 = 6; \y2 =0; 
			\x3 = 0; \y3 =0;
			\x4 = 9; \y4 =0; 
			\x5 = 0; \y5 =2.5; 
			\x6 = 9; \y6 =2.5; 
			\x7 = 0; \y7 =5.5;
			\x8 = 3; \y8 =8.5;
			\x9 = 3; \y9 =11.5;}
    \begin{center}
    \begin{tikzpicture}
	\draw[dashed] (\x5+0,\y5+0) --(\x5+2,\y5+0) --(\x5+2,\y5+2) --(\x5+0,\y5+2) --(\x5+0,\y5+0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x5+1.4,\y5+2) to (\x5+1.4,\y5+1) to[out=270,in=0] (\x5+1.2,\y5+0.8) to[out=180,in=270] (\x5+1,\y5+1) to[out=90, in=0] (\x5+0.8,\y5+1.2);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x5+1.2,\y5+0) to (\x5+1.2,\y5+0.8);
	\draw[green, line width=0.35mm] (\x5+0.8,\y5+0) to (\x5+0.8,\y5+2);
	
	\node at (\x5+2.5,\y5+1) {$=$};
	
	\draw[dashed] (\x5+3,\y5+0) --(\x5+5,\y5+0) --(\x5+5,\y5+2) --(\x5+3,\y5+2) --(\x5+3,\y5+0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x5+4.4,\y5+0) to (\x5+4.4,\y5+1) to[out=90,in=0] (\x5+4.2,\y5+1.2) to[out=180,in=90] (\x5+4,\y5+1) to[out=270,in=0] (\x5+3.8,\y5+0.8);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x5+4.2,\y5+2) to (\x5+4.2,\y5+1.2);
	\draw[green, line width=0.35mm] (\x5+3.8,\y5+0) to (\x5+3.8,\y5+2);

	We can also think of a 1-morphism in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ as a bimodule over special non-unital non-counital Frobenius algebras with $\vartriangleleft$ and $\rho$ being the the right (co)action and $\vartriangleright$ and $\lambda$ being the left (co)action.
	\item A 2-morphism between $(f,\vartriangleleft_f,\rho_f,\vartriangleright_f,\lambda_f)$ and $(g,\vartriangleleft_g,\rho_g,\vartriangleright_g,\lambda_g)$ is a 2-morphism $\varphi:f\to g$ in $\mathbb{B}$ such that
	\begin{align*}
	& \varphi\cdot\vartriangleleft_f=\vartriangleleft_g\cdot(\varphi\circ\textup{id}_p), \ (\varphi\circ\textup{id}_p)\cdot\rho_f=\rho_g\cdot\varphi, \\
	& \varphi\cdot\vartriangleright_f=\vartriangleright_g\cdot(\textup{id}_q\circ \varphi) \text{ and } (\textup{id}_q\circ\varphi)\cdot\lambda_f=\lambda_g\cdot \varphi.
	\end{align*}
	This can be graphically represented in the following way:

	\item Vertical composition, i.e., composition of 2-morphisms is simply given by the composition of 2-morphisms in $\mathbb{B}$. It follows that identity 2-morphisms are given by the identity 2-morphisms in $\mathbb{B}$. This turns $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,B_q)$ into a category.
	\item Composition of 1-morphisms (or horizontal composition) is defined as follows. Let $f:A_p\to B_q$ and $g:B_q\to C_r$ be 1-morphisms in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$. We can now form the idempotent
	\begin{align*}
	\kappa_{g\circ f}=(\textup{id}_g\circ \vartriangleright_f)\cdot(\rho_g\circ\textup{id}_f)=(\vartriangleleft_g\circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot(\textup{id}_g\circ \lambda_f):g\circ f\to g\circ f.
	\end{align*}		
	We define the composition of $f$ and $g$ as the splitting of this idempotent. We can graphically check that these two ways of writing this morphism do in fact coincide and that it forms an idempotent.

	We can now define right-$p$ (co)actions, and left-$r$ (co)actions on $g\otimes_q f$ as follows:
	\tikzmath{\x1 = 0; \y1 =2.5; 
		\x2 = 6; \y2 =2.5; 
		\x3 = 0; \y3 =0; 
		\x4 = 6; \y4 = 0; }

	This in fact turns it into a morphism $g\otimes_q f:A_p\to C_r$. Horizontal composition of 2-morphisms is defined in the following way:

	This turns composition into a functor
	\begin{align*}
	c_{A_p,B_q,C_r}:\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(B_q,C_r)\times\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,B_q)\to \textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,C_r).
	\end{align*}	
	It is important to note here that when defining the idempotent completion of a given bicategory $\mathbb{B}$, we have to make a choice for each pair of morphisms to be able to define this functor. All possible choices will lead to equivalent bicategories, but we have to make these choices none the less. 
	
	Let $D_s$ be another object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ and $h:C_r\to D_s$ another 1-morphism. The 1-morphisms $(h\otimes_r g)\otimes_q f:A_p\to D_s$ and  $h\otimes_r (g\otimes_q f):A_p\to D_s$ are now both splittings of the idempotent given by
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tikzpicture}
	\draw[dashed] (0,0) --(2,0) --(2,2) --(0,2) --(0,0);
	\draw[magenta, line width=0.35mm] (1,0) to (1,2);
	\node[right] at (1,1.5) {$h$};
	\node[right] at (0,1) {$D$};

	\draw[dashed] (3,0) --(5,0) --(5,2) --(3,2) --(3,0);
	\draw[red, line width=0.35mm] (3.6,0.5) to[out=0,in=270] (3.8,0.7) to (3.8,1.3) to[out=90,in=180] (4,1.5);
	\draw[blue, line width=0.35mm] (4,0.5) to[out=0,in=270] (4.2,0.7) to (4.2,1.3) to[out=90,in=180] (4.4,1.5);
	\draw[magenta, line width=0.35mm] (3.6,0) to (3.6,2);
	\draw[orange, line width=0.35mm] (4,0) to (4,2);
	\draw[green, line width=0.35mm] (4.4,0) to (4.4,2);
	\end{tikzpicture}
	\end{center}
	and thus we have a unique isomorphism $a_{h,g,f}:(h\otimes_r g)\otimes_q f\to h\otimes_r (g\otimes_q f)$ and in general we get a natural isomorphism
	\begin{align*}
	a_{A_p,B_q,C_r,D_s} : & c_{A_p,B_q,D_s}(c_{B_q,C_r,D_s}\times \textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,B_q)}) \\
	& \to c_{A_p,C_r,D_s}(\textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(C_r,D_s)}\times c_{A_p,B_q,C_r}).
	\end{align*}
	\item The identity 1-morphism on $A_p$ is given by $(p,m_p,\Delta_p,m_p,\Delta_p)$. Let $f:A_p\to B_q$ and $g:C_r\to A_p$ be 1-morphism. We now have the following:

	\node[right] at (\x1+6,\y1+1) {$A$};

	\draw[dashed] (\x2+0,\y2+0) --(\x2+2,\y2+0) --(\x2+2,\y2+2) --(\x2+0,\y2+2) --(\x2+0,\y2+0);
	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x2+0.8,\y2+0.5) to[out=0,in=270] (\x2+1,\y2+0.7) to (\x2+1,\y2+1.3) to[out=90,in=180] (\x2+1.2,\y2+1.5);

	\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x2+9.8,\y2+2) to (\x2+9.8,\y2+1.9) to[out=270,in=180] (\x2+10.2,\y2+1.5);
	\draw[orange, line width=0.35mm] (\x2+10.2,\y2+0) to (\x2+10.2,\y2+2);

	Since splittings are unique up to unique isomorphism, we have isomorphisms $l_g: p\otimes_p g\to g$ and $r_f:f\otimes_p p \to f$. These form natural isomorphism
	\begin{align*}
	& l_{C_r,A_p}:c_{C_r,A_p,A_p}(p,-)\to \textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(C_r,A_p)} \text{ and} \\
	& r_{A_p,B_q}:c_{A_p,A_p,B_q}(-,p)\to \textup{id}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(A_p,B_q)}.
	\end{align*}
	\item Since both the associator and left and right unitors are given by unique isomorphisms between colimits, it follows immediately that the triangle and pentagon axiom both have to hold.
\end{itemize}

<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{kar2com}
For every locally idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{B}$, the bicategory $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is 2-idempotent complete.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We first need to show that $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is locally idempotent complete. Let $A_p$ and $B_q$ be objects in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$, $(h,\vartriangleleft_h,\rho_h,\vartriangleright_h,\lambda_h):A_p\to B_q$ a 1-morphism and $e:h\to h$ an idempotent 2-morphism. Since $\mathbb{B}$ is locally idempotent complete, we know that the idempotent $e$ splits into 2-morphisms $f:h\to s$ and $g:s\to h$ such that $gf=e$ and $fg=\textup{id}_s$ where $s:A\to B$ is a 1-morphism in $\mathbb{B}$. Note that, a priori, $s$ is not a morphism in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ but we can turn $s$ into a morphism $s:A_p\to B_q$ with the following left and right (co)action:

\tikzmath{\x1 = 1.5; \y1 =8; 
	\x2 = 0; \y2 =5.5;
	\x3 = 0; \y3 =2.5;
	\x4 = 0; \y4 =0;}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\draw[dashed] (\x1+0,\y1+0) --(\x1+2,\y1+0) --(\x1+2,\y1+2) --(\x1+0,\y1+2) --(\x1+0,\y1+0);
\draw[line width=0.35mm] (\x1+1,\y1+0) to (\x1+1,\y1+2);
\node[right] at (\x1+1,\y1+1.5) {$p$};
\node[right] at (\x1,\y1+1) {$A$};
\node[left] at (\x1+2,\y1+1) {$A$};
	
\draw[dashed] (\x1+3,\y1+0) --(\x1+5,\y1+0) --(\x1+5,\y1+2) --(\x1+3,\y1+2) --(\x1+3,\y1+0);
\draw[blue, line width=0.35mm] (\x1+4,\y1+0) to (\x1+4,\y1+2);
\node[right] at (\x1+4,\y1+1.5) {$q$};
\node[right] at (\x1+3,\y1+1) {$B$};

With this definition of $s$, $f$ and $g$ also become 2-morphisms in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ and therefore split the idempotent $e$. Thus $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is locally idempotent complete.

Now, let $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ be an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ and $(e,\vartriangleleft,\rho,\vartriangleright,\lambda)$ a 2-idempotent on $A_p$, which means we have morphisms $m^\otimes_e:e\otimes_p e\to e$ and $\Delta^\otimes_e:e\to e\otimes_p e$ such that
\begin{align*}
(\textup{id}_e\otimes_p m^\otimes_e)\cdot(\Delta^\otimes_e\otimes_p \textup{id}_e) & =(m^\otimes_e\otimes_p \textup{id}_e)\cdot(\textup{id}_e\otimes_p\Delta^\otimes_e)=\Delta^\otimes_e\cdot m^\otimes_e \text{ and} \\
m^\otimes_e\cdot\Delta^\otimes_e & =\textup{id}_e.
\end{align*}
We want to show that this 2-idempotent splits. From the definition of $e\otimes_p e$ we have 2-morphisms $\varphi:e\circ e\to e\otimes_p e$ and $\psi:e\otimes_p e\to e\circ e$ such that $\varphi\cdot\psi=\textup{id}_{e\otimes_p e}$ and $\psi\cdot\varphi=\kappa_{e\circ e}$.

Combining these we get morphisms $m_e=m_e^\otimes\cdot\varphi:e\circ e\to e$ and $\Delta_e=\psi\cdot\Delta_e^\otimes:e\to e\circ e$. Graphically, we can represent these in the following way:

Therefore $(A,e,m_e,\Delta_e)$ is an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ and furthermore we can now define morphisms $(e,\vartriangleleft,\rho,m_e,\Delta_e):A_p\to A_e$ and $(e,m_e\Delta_e,\vartriangleright,\lambda):A_e\to A_p$. Composing them in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$, we get $e\otimes_e e\,\cong\, e:A_p\to A_p$ and $e\otimes_p e:A_e\to A_e$. As we have morphisms $m_e^\otimes: e\otimes_p e \to e=\textup{id}_{A_e}$ and $\Delta_e^\otimes: \textup{id}_{A_e}=e\to e\otimes_p e$, we have shown that $(e,\vartriangleleft,\rho,\vartriangleright,\lambda)$ splits in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ and thus $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is 2-idempotent complete.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{x3}
For any object $A_p$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$, $A_p$ is a splitting of the 2-idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}$.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{kar2emb}
For every locally idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{B}$, there exists a fully faithful pseudofunctor $\iota_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$. If $\mathbb{B}$ is furthermore 2-idempotent complete, this functor is an equivalence.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We define $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ to map the object $A$ in $\mathbb{B}$ onto $(A,\textup{id}_A,\textup{id}_{\textup{id}_A},\textup{id}_{\textup{id}_A})$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$. It maps 1-morphisms $f:A\to B$ in $\mathbb{B}$ onto the the morphism $(f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f):A_{\textup{id}}\to B_{\textup{id}}$ and 2-morphisms $\varphi:f\to g$ in $\mathbb{B}$ onto $\varphi:f\to g$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$.

We now note that, for objects $A$, $B$ in $\mathbb{B}$, every morphism in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ between $A_{\textup{id}}$ and $B_{\textup{id}}$ is of the form $(f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f)$ where $f$ is an arbitrary morphism $f:A\to B$ in $\mathbb{B}$. Since a 2-morphism between 1-morphisms of the form  $(f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f)$ and $(g,\textup{id}_g,\textup{id}_g,\textup{id}_g,\textup{id}_g)$ is also just an arbitrary 2-morphism $\varphi:f\to g$, we see that $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is fully faithful.

Now assume that $\mathbb{B}$ is 2-idempotent complete and let $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ be an object in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$. We want to show that $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is essentially surjective, i.e., there exists some $B$ in $\mathbb{B}$ such that $A_p\,\simeq\, \iota_\mathbb{B} B$. We know that the 2-idempotent $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ splits in $\mathbb{B}$, which means there exists an object $B$ in $\mathbb{B}$, 1-morphisms $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to A$, 2-morphisms $\varphi:f\circ g\to \textup{id}_B$, $\psi:\textup{id}_B \to f\circ g$ and an isomorphism $\gamma:g\circ f\to p$ such that $m=\gamma\cdot(\textup{id}_g \circ \varphi \circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot(\gamma^{-1}\circ\gamma^{-1})$ and $\Delta=(\gamma\circ\gamma)\cdot(\textup{id}_g \circ \psi \circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot\gamma^{-1}$.

We can now define the morphisms
\begin{align*}
& (f,(\varphi\circ\textup{id}_f)\cdot(\textup{id}_f\circ \gamma^{-1}),(\textup{id}_f\circ\gamma)\cdot(\psi\circ\textup{id}_f),\textup{id}_f,\textup{id}_f):A_p\to B_{\textup{id}} \text{ and} \\
& (g,\textup{id}_g,\textup{id}_g,(\textup{id}_g\circ\varphi)\cdot(\gamma^{-1}\circ\textup{id}_g),(\gamma\circ\textup{id}_g)\cdot(\textup{id}_g\circ\psi)):B_{\textup{id}}\to A_p
\end{align*}
and, with these, we now have $g\otimes_{\textup{id}_B} f\,\cong\, g\circ f\,\cong\, p=\textup{id}_{A_p}$ and $f\otimes_p g\,\cong\,\textup{id}_B$. Thus it follows that $A_p\,\simeq\, B_{\textup{id}}$ and $\iota_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$ is an equivalence of bicategories.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{lscol}
For each locally idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ and 2-idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{C}$, we have an equivalence of bicategories
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B}),\mathbb{C})\simeq\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{C})
\end{align*}
induced by precomposing with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
First, we want to show that for every pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$, there exists a pseudofunctor $F^\prime:\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $F^\prime\iota_\mathbb{B}\,\simeq\, F$, i.e., precomposition with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is essentially surjective. For a given pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{B}\to \mathbb{C}$ we can define the pseu\-do\-functor $\textup{Kar}(F):\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\to\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{C})$ which maps a 2-idempotent $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ onto the 2-idempotent $(F(A),F(p),F(m),F(\Delta))$ and acts analogously on 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms. The following diagram now commutes up to equivalence
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
\mathbb{B} \arrow[r, "F"] \arrow[d, "\iota_\mathbb{B}"] & \mathbb{C} \arrow[d, "\iota_\mathbb{C}"] \\
\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B}) \arrow[r, "\textup{Kar}(F)"]            & \textup{Kar}(\mathbb{C})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
Since $\mathbb{C}$ is a 2-idempotent complete bicategory, $\iota_\mathbb{C}$ is an equivalence and we can choose an inverse $\iota_\mathbb{C}{^{-1}}$. We now define $F^\prime=\iota_\mathbb{C}{^{-1}}\textup{Kar}(F)$ and have 
\begin{align*}
F^\prime\iota_\mathbb{B}=\iota_\mathbb{C}{^{-1}}\textup{Kar}(F)\iota_\mathbb{B}\,\simeq\, \iota_\mathbb{C}{^{-1}}\iota_\mathbb{C} F\,\simeq\, F.
\end{align*}

Secondly, we need to show that precomposition with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is essentially surjective on Hom-categories. Let $F,G:\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\to\mathbb{C}$ be pseudofunctors. We want to show that for each strong transformation $\varphi:F\iota_\mathbb{B}\to G\iota_\mathbb{B}$, we can find a strong transformation $\varphi^\prime:F\to G$ such that $\varphi^\prime\iota_\mathbb{B}\,\cong\, \varphi$. For a given $\varphi:F\iota_\mathbb{B}\to G\iota_\mathbb{B}$, we define such a $\varphi^\prime$ by defining an idempotent and then setting $\varphi^\prime_{A_p}$ to be its splitting. This idempotent $\gamma_{A_p}:G(p)\varphi_A F(p)\to G(p)\varphi_A F(p)$ is given via
\begin{center}

\end{center}
and we now have a splitting consisting of $\varphi^\prime_{A_p}:F(A_p)\to G(A_p)$ along with morphisms $\alpha_{A_p}:G(p)\varphi_A F(p)\to \varphi^\prime_{A_p}$ and $\beta_{A_p}:\varphi^\prime_{A_p}\to G(p)\varphi_A F(p)$ which satisfy $\alpha_{A_p} \beta_{A_p} =\textup{id}_{\varphi^\prime_{A_p}}$ and $\beta_{A_p} \alpha_{A_p}=\gamma_{A_p}$. We define $\varphi^\prime_f$ on a morphism $f:A_p\to B_q$ via

where the top morphism is given by the image of

under $F$ and the bottom morphism is given by the image of

\draw[blue, line width=0.35mm] (0.75,2) to (0.75,1.5) to[out=270,in=180] (1,1.25);

under $G$. This turns $\varphi^\prime:G\to F$ into a strong transformation. We now need to show that $\varphi^\prime\iota_\mathbb{B}\,\cong\,\varphi$, i.e., $\varphi^\prime_{A_{\textup{id}}}\,\cong\, \varphi_A$. If we look at the idempotent $\gamma_{A_{\textup{id}}}$ we see that it splits via $\varphi_A$ and thus $\varphi^\prime_{A_{\textup{id}}}\,\cong\, \varphi_A$.

Lastly, we need to show that precomposition with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is fully faithful on Hom-categories. Let $F,G:\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\to\mathbb{C}$ be pseudofunctors and $\varphi,\psi:F\to G$ strong transformations. We want to show that we have an isomorphism
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B}),\mathbb{C})(F,G)(\varphi,\psi)\,\cong\, \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{C})(F\iota_\mathbb{B},G\iota_\mathbb{B})(\varphi\iota_\mathbb{B},\psi\iota_\mathbb{B}).
\end{align*}
Let $\Gamma:\varphi\iota_\mathbb{B}\to \psi\iota_\mathbb{B}$ be a modification. We can construct a modification $\Gamma^\prime:\varphi\to\psi$ with components $\Gamma^\prime_{A_p}:\varphi_{A_p}\to\psi_{A_p}$ via the following.

This defines a modification $\Gamma^\prime:F\to G$ and we can see that this construction defines an inverse on the level of modifications. Thus precomposition with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is fully faithful on Hom-categories and we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B}),\mathbb{C})\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{C}).
\end{align*}

<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Without going into technical details, theorem \ref{lscol} is a consequence of the fact that idempotent completion should form a left adjoint trifunctor $\textup{Kar}:{\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}_\textup{lic}}\to{\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}_\textup{ic}}$ from the tricategory of locally idempotent complete bicategories, pseudofunctors, strong transformations and modifications into the full subtricategory of 2-idempotent complete bicategories, analogously to theorem \ref{1adj}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
{(Weighted Colimit)}
Let $\mathbb{J}$ and $\mathbb{B}$ be bicategories. Given a presheaf $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$, which we will call \textit{weight}, and another pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$, the \textit{colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$} is given in the following way: We can form the pseudofunctor
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F,-)):\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}.
\end{align*}
If this pseudofunctor is representable, i.e., there exists an object $\textup{colim}^W F$ and an equivalence of pseudofunctors $\varphi:\mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}^W F,-)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F,-))$, we call $\textup{colim}^W F$ together with $\varphi$ the \textit{colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$} or just the \textit{weighted colimit of $F$} and we call $\varphi$ a \textit{universal} strong transformation.

By the Yoneda Lemma, the data of this strong transformation is equivalent to the object $\varphi_{\textup{colim}^W F}(\textup{id}_{\textup{colim}^W F})$ in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F))$, i.e., a strong transformation $\lambda:W\to \mathbb{B}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F)$ such that precomposition with $\lambda$ defines an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\lambda^*:\mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}^W F,-)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F,-)).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
{(Cocomplete Bicategory)}
A bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ is called \textit{cocomplete} if for every weight $W$ and every pseudofunctor $F$ into $\mathbb{B}$ the weighted colimit of $F$ by $W$ exists.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
{(Preservation of Weighted Colimits)}
Let $\mathbb{C}$ be another bicategory and $G:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$ a pseudofunctor. We say $G$ \textit{preserves} a colimit if precomposition with $G\lambda:W\to \mathbb{C}(GF-,G\textup{colim}^W F)$ defines an equivalence
\begin{align*}
(G\lambda)^*:\mathbb{C}(G\textup{colim}^W F,-)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{C}(GF,-)).
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
{(Absolute Weighted Colimit)}
A weighted colimit is called \textit{absolute} if it is preserved by every pseudofunctor.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
{(Absolute Weight)}
A weight $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ is called \textit{absolute} if for every bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ and every pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$, the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ is absolute if it exists.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
{(Weighted Colimits in Locally $P$ Bicategories)} \label{lPcolim}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally $P$ bicategory, $\mathbb{J}$ an arbitrary bicategory and $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$ a pseudofunctor. A \textit{$P$-weight} is a presheaf $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_P$. The \textit{$P$-weighted colimit} of $F$ weighted by $W$ now consists of a strong transformation $\lambda:W\to\mathbb{B}(F-,\textup{colim}_P^W F)$ such that
\begin{align*}
\lambda^*:\mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}_P^W F,b)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_{P}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F,b))
\end{align*}
defines an equivalence of categories for all objects $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$. A locally $P$ bicategory is called \textit{$P$-cocomplete} if every $P$-weighted colimit exists.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory, the 2-categories $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})$ are cocomplete.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{spd2idcomp}
The free walking 2-idempotent splitting is locally idempotent complete.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
We have to show that all Hom-categories of $\spadesuit_2$ are idempotent complete. Since there are only 4 of them, we can check this by hand. The objects of $\spadesuit_2(Y,Y)$ are generated by $fg:Y\to Y$. The only non-identity idempotent on $fg$ is $\psi\varphi$ which splits trivially via $\varphi$ and $\psi$. This shows that $\spadesuit_2(Y,Y)$ is idempotent complete.

We have an equivalence of categories $f^*:\spadesuit_2(Y,Y)\to\spadesuit_2(X,Y)$, since all 1-morphisms $h:X\to Y$ can be written as $h^\prime \circ f$ for some $h^\prime:Y\to Y$, and all 2-morphisms $\alpha:h^\prime \circ f\to k^\prime \circ f$ are of the form $\alpha^\prime \circ \textup{id}_f$, for some $\alpha^\prime:h^\prime \to k^\prime:Y\to Y$. This implies that $\spadesuit_2(X,Y)$ is idempotent complete. We get an analogous equivalence and result for $\spadesuit_2(Y,X)$.

For $\spadesuit_2(X,X)$ we do not get an equivalence but we note that all 1-morphisms $h:X\to X$ except $\textup{id}_X$ can be written as $g\circ h^\prime\circ f$ for some $h^\prime:Y\to Y$. Since the only 2-morphism on $\textup{id}_X$ is the identity, and there are no 2-morphisms between $\textup{id}_X$ and any other 1-morphism, idempotent completeness of $\spadesuit_2(Y,Y)$ still implies the idempotent completeness of $\spadesuit_2(X,X)$. Thus $\spadesuit_2$ is locally idempotent complete.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally idempotent complete bicategory and $(A,p,m,\Delta)$ a 2-idempotent which corresponds to a pseudofunctor $F:\clubsuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$. The colimit of $F$ weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y):\clubsuit_2^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ determines a splitting of $A_p$ and every splitting determines a colimit of $F$ weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
First we note that from this point onward we are interested in weighted colimits in locally idempotent complete bicategories as laid out in definition \ref{lPcolim}. We will shorten "idempotent complete" to ic, whenever appropriate when talking about weighted colimits in locally idempotent complete bicategories.

We note that lemma \ref{spd2idcomp} implies that the weight $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y):\clubsuit_2^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ takes values in idempotent complete categories and defines an ic-weight. Assume that the colimit of $F$ weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)$ exists. The colimit of $F$ weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,X)\,\simeq\, \clubsuit_2(-,X)$ exists trivially and is equivalent to $FX$ by the Yoneda lemma. Proposition \ref{ext} tells us that the existence of these weighted colimits guarantees the existence of an extension $F^\prime:\spadesuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$ of $F$ along $\iota:\clubsuit_2\to \spadesuit_2$ such that $F^\prime\iota \,\simeq\, F$. By remark \ref{ExtIsSplit}, this shows that the colimit of $F$ weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)$ determines a splitting of $A_p$.

Before we can finish this proof, we briefly examine the bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\clubsuit_2^\textup{op},\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic})$ to better understand colimits weighted by $\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)$. For a given monoidal category $\mathcal{C}$, we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}((\textup{B}\mathcal{C})^\textup{op},\textbf{\textup{Cat}})\,\simeq\,\mathbb{A}\textup{ct-}\mathcal{C}
\end{align*}
where $\textup{B}\mathcal{C}$ is the delooping of $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathbb{A}\textup{ct-}\mathcal{C}$ is the bicategory of categories with a right $\mathcal{C}$-action,
given by evaluating at the one object of $\textup{B}\mathcal{C}$. This is a categorification of the fact that, for a monoid $M$, there is an equivalence between $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{B} M^\textup{op}, \textbf{\textup{Set}})$ and the category of sets with a right $M$-action. Analogously, its proof consists of correctly de- and reassembling the data of the pseudofunctors in question. Further details on actions of monoidal categories on categories can be found in \cite{CG}.

Since $\clubsuit_2$ is a one-object bicategory, we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\clubsuit_2^\textup{op},\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic})\,\simeq\,\mathbb{A}\textup{ct-}\clubsuit_2(X,X).
\end{align*}
Thus, a strong transformation $\kappa:\spadesuit_2(\iota -, Y)\to \mathbb{B}(F-,C):\clubsuit_2^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ corresponds to a functor $\kappa_X:\spadesuit_2(X, Y)\to \mathbb{B}(A,C)$ preserving the action of $\clubsuit_2(X,X)$. We can now show that $\kappa$ is uniquely up to unique isomorphism determined by $\kappa_X(f)$ together with a right $p$-module structure on it. The following diagram commutes up to isomorphism.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\spadesuit_2(X,Y)\times \clubsuit_2(X,X)} \arrow[r, "\kappa_X\times\textup{id}"] \arrow[d, "\textup{id}\times\iota"] & {\mathbb{B}(A,C)\times\clubsuit_2(X,X)} \arrow[d, "\textup{id}\times F"] \\
{\spadesuit_2(X,Y)\times \spadesuit_2(X,X)} \arrow[d, "\circ"]                                         & {\mathbb{B}(A,C)\times\mathbb{B}(A,A)} \arrow[d, "\circ"]          \\
{\spadesuit_2(X,Y)} \arrow[r, "\kappa_X"]                                                        & {\mathbb{B}(A,C)}                                          
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
We therefore have $\kappa_X(f\circ h)\,\cong\,\kappa_X(f) \circ F(h)$ and $\kappa_X(\textup{id}_f\circ \alpha)\,\cong\, \textup{id}_{\kappa_X(f)}\circ F(\alpha)$ for $h$ a 1-morphism and $\alpha$ a 2-morphism in $\mathbb{B}(A,A)$. The 2-morphisms in $\spadesuit_2(X,Y)$ which cannot be written as $\textup{id}_f \circ \alpha$ are all generated by $\varphi^{\circ n}\circ \textup{id}_f$ and $\psi^{\circ n}\circ \textup{id}_f$. Though, we note that
\begin{align*}
\kappa_X(\varphi^{\circ 2}\circ \textup{id}_f)\,\cong\, \kappa_X((\varphi\circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot (\textup{id}_f\circ\textup{id}_g\circ\varphi\circ\textup{id}_f))\,\cong\, \kappa_X(\varphi\circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot \left(\textup{id}_{\kappa_X(f)}\circ F(\textup{id}_g\circ \varphi\circ \textup{id}_f)\right),
\end{align*}
i.e., all of these are up to isomorphism determined by $\kappa_X(\varphi\circ \textup{id}_f):f\circ p\to f$ and $\kappa_X(\psi\circ \textup{id}_f):f\to f\circ p$ which need to satisfy $\kappa_X(\varphi\circ \textup{id}_f)\cdot\kappa_X(\psi\circ \textup{id}_f)=\textup{id}_{\kappa_X(f)}$, i.e., a right $p$-action on $\kappa_X(f)$.

Now let $(A,B,f,g,\varphi,\psi,\gamma)$ be a splitting of $A_p$, determining an extension $F^\prime$ of $F$. We can define a strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda:\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)\to \mathbb{B}(F-,B)
\end{align*}
by defining $\lambda_X:\spadesuit_2(X,Y)\to \mathbb{B}(A,B)$ to be $F^\prime$. We now need to show that it is universal, i.e.,
\begin{align*}
\lambda^*:\mathbb{B}(B,b)\to \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\clubsuit_2,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic})(\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y),\mathbb{B}(F-,b))
\end{align*}
defines an equivalence of categories for each object $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$. Let $\kappa:\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y)\to \mathbb{B}(F-,b)$ be another strong transformation which is determined by the right $p$-module $\kappa_X(f):A\to b$. We can now form the morphism $\kappa_X(f)\otimes_p g:B\to b$ and will now show that this defines an inverse to $\lambda^*$. We have
\begin{align*}
(\kappa_X(f)\otimes_p g)\lambda_X(f)=(\kappa_X(f)\otimes_p g)f \,\cong\, \kappa_X(f)\otimes_p (gf)\,\cong\, \kappa_X(f)\otimes_p p\,\cong\, \kappa_X(f)
\end{align*}
and since the composition with $\lambda_X(f)$ is a composite of $\textup{id}_B$-modules, this isomorphism also preserves the right $p$-module structure and $(\kappa_X(f)\otimes_p g)\lambda \,\cong\, \kappa$. Furthermore, for a morphism $h:B\to b$, we have
\begin{align*}
\left(h\lambda_X(f)\right) \otimes_p g\,\cong\, (hf)\otimes_p g \,\cong\, h(f\otimes_p g) \,\cong\, h\textup{id}_B\,\cong\, h.
\end{align*}
Thus $\lambda$ is universal.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{x4}
Any two splittings of the same 2-idempotent are equivalent in a locally idempotent complete bicategory.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
$\spadesuit_2(\iota-,Y):\clubsuit_2^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is an absolute ic-weight.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory. The bicategories $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$, $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ are 2-idempotent complete.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Corollaries \ref{Catlic} and \ref{Pshlic} tell us that $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$, $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ are all locally idempotent complete. By theorem \ref{x2} and corollary \ref{Pshicc} we know that $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ are ic-cocomplete. Since splittings of a 2-idempotents are given by an ic-weighted colimit, they are also 2-idempotent complete.

One can show, that the data of a 2-idempotent in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ is the same data as that of a 2-idempotent in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and furthermore a splitting of this idempotent in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ defines a splitting of it in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and vice versa. This implies that $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ is also 2-idempotent complete.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
{(Cauchy Completion)}
We call an object $A$ in a locally idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ \textit{atomic} if the pseudofunctor $\mathbb{B}(A,-):\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is ic-cocontinuous, i.e., preserves all ic-weighted colimits.

Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally idempotent complete bicategory. The \textit{Cauchy completion} of $\mathbb{B}$ is defined to be the full subbicategory of atomic objects in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$, i.e., an object in this bicategory is a pseudofunctor $S:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ such that $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,-):\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is ic-cocontinuous. We will denote this bicategory as $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
We will frequently use the formula
\begin{align*}
\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F \,\simeq\, \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} Wj \times Fj
\end{align*}
to calculate weighted colimits using coends. This equation is not explicitly written anywhere in \cite{Lor} for bicategorical coends but it follows just the same as its 1-categorical counterpart.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{repato2}
Representable presheaves are atomic.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let $b$ be an object in $\mathbb{B}$, we will now show that $\mathbb{B}(-,b)$ is atomic. Let $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ be a pseudofunctor and $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ a weight with colimit $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F$, i.e., we have a universal strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda:W\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(F-,\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F).
\end{align*}
and we will now see that $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(\mathbb{B}(-,b),-)$ preserves this colimit. Applying this functor to $\lambda$ yields a strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda_* :W \to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(\mathbb{B}(-,b),F-),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(\mathbb{B}(-,b),\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F)).
\end{align*}
Via the Yoneda lemma, the strong transformation $\lambda_*$ corresponds to the strong transformation $\lambda_b:W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(F(-)(b),\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F(b))$. Since weighted colimits in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ are computed point-wise, we know that $\lambda_b$ has to define a weighted colimit which implies that $\lambda_*$ is universal as well. Thus the pseudofunctor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(\mathbb{B}(-,b),-)$ preserves colimits and $\mathbb{B}(b,-)$ is atomic.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{absato2}
Let $\mathbb{J}$ be a locally idempotent complete bicategory. An ic-weight $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is absolute if and only if is atomic as an object in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
To start, let $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ be an absolute weight. To show that $W$ is atomic, let $V:\mathbb{I}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ be another weight and $F:\mathbb{I}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})$ a pseudofunctor with colimit $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V F$. We have
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V F) &\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{J}}, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V F) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{J}}, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V F) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{J}},F) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{J}},F) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,F).
\end{align*}
For the first equivalence, we use the density formula, for the second the absoluteness of $W$, for the third we use Proposition \ref{repato2}, for the fourth we use the fact that $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^V:{\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}_\textup{lic}}(\mathbb{I},\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic})\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ defines a functor, and lastly the absoluteness of $W$ again. This shows that $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,-):\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is ic-cocontinuous and therefore $W$ is atomic.

We note that by moving $\textup{colim}^W$ to the outside, it defines a weighted colimit in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$, i.e., a weighted limit in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ since the left argument of the Hom-functor is contravariant.

Now let $W$ be atomic. Let $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$ be a functor. The colimit $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F$ satisfies the following:
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F, b) &\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\mathbb{B}(F-,b)) \,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\mathbb{B}(F-,b)}\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\mathbb{B}(F-,b)}\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}),
\end{align*}  
for an arbitrary $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$, where we used the atomicity of $W$ to pull out the colimit. For brevity, we use $W^\textup{co}$ to denote $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}):\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$. Now let $G:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$ be an arbitrary functor, and $c$ an object in $\mathbb{C}$. Using coends, we have
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{C}(G\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F, c) &\,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \mathbb{C}(Gb,c)\times \mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F,b) \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \mathbb{C}(Gb,c)\times \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} \mathbb{B}(Fj,b) \times W^\textup{co} (j) \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} \mathbb{C}(Gb,c)\times \mathbb{B}(Fj,b) \times W^\textup{co} (j) \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \mathbb{C}(Gb,c)\times \mathbb{B}(Fj,b) \times W^\textup{co} (j) \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} \mathbb{C}(GFj,c) \times W^\textup{co} (j) \,\simeq\, \mathbb{C}(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W GF, c)
\end{align*}
where we used the Yoneda lemma as stated in \cite[7.1.2 (7.28)]{Lor} for the first and fifth equivalences. By the Yoneda lemma, we now have $G\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W GF$. This shows that colimits weighted by $W$ are preserved by arbitrary functors, thus $W$ is an absolute weight.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{cau2com}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally idempotent complete bicategory. Its Cauchy completion $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is complete under icAWCs.
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Let $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ be an absolute weight and $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ a pseudofunctor. A priori, the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ does not need to exist in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ but since $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is ic-cocomplete, it will exist there. We now need to show that this colimit defines an atomic object. For this we will use Proposition \ref{absato2}, i.e., we will show that this colimit is an absolute weight. Let $G:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a pseudofunctor such that its colimit weighted by $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F$ exists. We have the following equivalence: 
\begin{align*}
\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F} G &\,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W Fb \times Gb \,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} Wj \times F(j)(b) \times Gb \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} Wj \times \int^{b : \mathbb{B}} F(j)(b) \times Gb \,\simeq\, \int^{j:\mathbb{J}} Wj \times \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{Fj} G  \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G
\end{align*}
Now let $H:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}$ be an arbitrary functor. Since $W$ is absolute and $F$ takes values in absolute weights, we have
\begin{align*}
H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G\right) \,\simeq\,  \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G\right) \,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F HG.
\end{align*}
Together, this yields
\begin{align*}
H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F} G\right) \,\cong\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F} HG.
\end{align*}
Therefore, $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^W F$ defines an absolute weight showing that $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathcal{C})$ is complete under icAWCs.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{cau2emb}
For every locally idempotent bicategory $\mathbb{B}$, the Yoneda embedding $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ takes values in $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ and thus defines a fully faithful pseudofunctor $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$. If $\mathbb{B}$ is furthermore complete under icAWCs, this pseudofunctor is an equivalence.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $b$ be an object in $\mathbb{B}$.  It follows from proposition \ref{repato2} that $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}(b)=\mathbb{B}(-,b)$ is atomic. Thus $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ defines a fully faithful pseudofunctor.

Now assume that $\mathbb{B}$ is complete under icAWCs. Let $S$ be an atomic presheaf on $\mathbb{B}$. By Proposition \ref{absato2}, $S$ is an absolute weight. By our assumption, the colimit of $\textup{id}_{\mathbb{B}}:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{B}$ weighted by $S:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ exists in $\mathbb{B}$. We now have that
\begin{align*}
