\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}} \, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \textup{id}_{\mathbb{B}} \,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}} \,\simeq\, S
\end{align*}
where the first equivalence follows by absoluteness and the second by the density formula. Therefore the pseudofunctor $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is essentially surjective and thus an equivalence of bicategories.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{EW2}
For any two locally idempotent complete bicategories $\mathbb{B}$, $\mathbb{C}$, we have an equivalence of categories
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})) \,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C}))
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
At its core, this proposition is a variant of the Eilenberg-Watts theorem named after the near simultaneous results of Eilenberg \cite{Eil} and  Watts \cite{Wat}. A more common version states that there is an equivalence of categories
\begin{align*}
\textup{Prof}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}) \,\simeq\, \textup{Func}^{\textup{coc}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C}),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{D}))
\end{align*}
between the category of profunctors from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{D}$, i.e., functors of the form $\mathcal{D}^\textup{op}\times\mathcal{C}\to\textbf{\textup{Set}}$, and the category of cocontinuous functors from $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{C})$ to $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathcal{D})$, for categories $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
To begin, we construct the pseudofunctor  
\begin{align*}
\Phi : \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})) \to \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C}))
\end{align*}
which maps a pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})$ to the pseudofunctor $\Phi_F:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})$ which is defines as
\begin{align*}
\Phi_F(S)(c)=\int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times F(b)(c). 
\end{align*}
It directly follows that this construction is functorial in $F$, $S$ and $c$, i.e., that $\Phi$, $\Phi_F$ and $\Phi_F(S)$ define pseudofunctors but we still need to verify that $\Phi_F(S)$ is an atomic presheaf. We do this via proposition \ref{absato2}, by checking that it is an absolute weight. Let $G:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{D}$ be an arbitrary pseudofunctor such that the colimit $\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\Phi_F(S)} G$ exists. We now have
\begin{align*}
\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\Phi_F(S)} G &\,\simeq\, \int^{c:\mathbb{C}} \Phi_F(S)(c) \times Gc \,\simeq\, \int^{c:\mathbb{C}} \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times F(b)(c) \times Gc \\
&\,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times \int^{c:\mathbb{C}} F(b)(c) \times Gc \,\simeq\, \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{Fb} G \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G. 
\end{align*}
It now follows, that for an arbitrary pseudofunctor $H$, we have
\begin{align*}
H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\Phi_F(S)} G\right) &\,\simeq\, H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G\right) \,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S H\left(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F G\right) \\
&\,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^F HG \,\simeq\, \textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^{\Phi_F(S)} HG
\end{align*}
since $S$ is an absolute weight and $F$ takes values in absolute weights, showing that $\Phi_F(S)$ is an atomic presheaf.

Next, the functor
\begin{align*}
F: \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{C})) \to \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{C}))
\end{align*}
which maps a pseudofunctor $\Phi:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})$ to a pseudofunctor $F_\Phi:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{C})$, is defined by precomposing with $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$.

We can now show that for any given $F:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{C})$ we have $F_{\Phi_F}\,\simeq\, F$ and for any given $\Phi:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{B})\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}(\mathbb{C})$ we have $\Phi_{F_{\Phi}}\,\simeq\, \Phi$. We will start with the first. Let $b^\prime$ in $\mathbb{B}$, and $c$ in $\mathbb{C}$ be objects, we have
\begin{align*}
F_{\Phi_F}(b^\prime)(c) &= \Phi_F(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}(b^\prime))(c) = \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}(b^\prime)(b) \times F(b)(c) \\
&= \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} \mathbb{B}(b,b^\prime) \times F(b)(c) \,\simeq\, F(b^\prime)(c)  
\end{align*}
where in the last step we used the Yoneda lemma as stated in \cite[7.1.2 (7.28)]{Lor}. Now let $S:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ be an atomic presheaf and $c$ in $\mathbb{C}$ an object. We have
\begin{align*}
\Phi_{F_{\Phi}}(S)(c) &= \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times F_{\Phi}(b)(c) = \int^{b:\mathbb{B}} Sb \times \Phi(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}(b))(c) \\
&\,\simeq\, (\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S \Phi(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}}))(c) \,\simeq\, \Phi(\textup{colim}_{\textup{ic}}^S\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\mathbb{B}})(c) \,\cong\, \Phi(S)(c)
\end{align*}
where we used that $S$ is an absolute weight.

Since both these equivalences are natural, this proves the desired equivalence 
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})) \,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{C})).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cau2equ}
For every locally idempotent bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ and 2-idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{C}$, there is an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}),\mathbb{C})\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{C})
\end{align*} 
given by precomposing with $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
This immediately follows from lemma \ref{EW2} together with proposition \ref{cau2emb}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{splitequiv}
A 2-retract of an equivalences is an equivalence, i.e., given two split 2-idempotents, i.e., pseudofunctors $F,G:\spadesuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$ and a strong transformation $\alpha:F\to G$, if $\alpha_X$ is an equivalence then so is $\alpha_Y$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let $\alpha_X^{-1}$ be an inverse to $\alpha_X$ up to isomorphism. The inverse of $\alpha_Y$ will be defined as $F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}G(g)$. For this, we need to define a right $G(p)$-module structure on $F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}$ where we use $p$ to denote $gf:X\to X$ in $\spadesuit_2$.

The isomorphism $\alpha_p:G(p)\alpha_X\to\alpha_X F(p)$ yields an isomorphism $\alpha_X^{-1}G(p)\,\cong\, F(p)\alpha_X^{-1}$. With this, we now have a right $G(p)$-action
\begin{align*}
F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}G(p)\,\cong\, F(f)F(p)\alpha_X^{-1}\,\cong\, F(fp)\alpha_X^{-1}\to F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}
\end{align*}
where the last arrow is given by $F(\varphi\circ\textup{id}_f)\circ\textup{id}_{\alpha_X^{-1}}$. Analogously, we can define a right $G(p)$-coaction. It follows from the naturality of $\alpha$ that this defines a right $G(p)$-module structure.

We can now define $F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}G(g)$ and show that it is inverse to $\alpha_Y$. We have
\begin{align*}
\alpha_Y F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}G(g) \,\cong\, G(f)\alpha_X \alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}G(g) & \,\cong\, G(f)\otimes_{G(p)}G(g)\,\cong\,\textup{id}_{GY} \text{  and} \\ 
F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}G(g)\alpha_Y \,\cong\, F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\otimes_{G(p)}\alpha_X F(g) & \,\cong\, F(f)\alpha_X^{-1}\alpha_X\otimes_{F(p)}F(g) \\
& \,\cong\, F(f)\otimes_{F(p)}F(g)\,\cong\, \textup{id}_{FY}
\end{align*}
where we used the fact that $f\otimes_p g\,\cong\, \textup{id}_Y$ at the end of both calculations as well as the fact that $\alpha_X$ freely translates between $F(p)$- and $G(p)$-module structures. This proves that $\alpha_Y$ is an equivalence.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{univnat}
Let $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$ be a pseudofunctor and $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ a weight such that $\textup{colim}^W F$ exists. We then have a canonical strong transformation
\begin{align*}
u:\textup{colim}^W \mathbb{B}(-,F) \to \mathbb{B}(-,\textup{colim}^W F):\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
First, we note that $\textup{colim}^W \mathbb{B}(-,F)$ exists since $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is cocomplete.
 
On objects we can define $u$ in the following way. For any $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$, we can define a strong transformation $W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B}(b,F),\mathbb{B}(b,\textup{colim}^W F))$ given by postcomposing with the universal strong transformation $\lambda:W\to \mathbb{B}(F,\textup{colim}^W F)$. This yields a functor $u_b: \textup{colim}^W \mathbb{B}(b,F) \to \mathbb{B}(b,\textup{colim}^W F)$ by universality. These functors assemble into the desired strong transformation $u$ with its component 2-isomorphisms given by universality.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{x7}
A 2-retract of an atomic object is atomic.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $A$ be an atomic object in $\mathbb{B}$ and $B$ a retract of $A$, i.e., we have a pseu\-do\-functor $F:\spadesuit_2\to\mathbb{B}$ such that $FX\,\simeq\, A$ and $FY \,\simeq\, B$. It follows from its definition that $\spadesuit_2$ is equivalent to its opposite $\spadesuit_2^\textup{op}$. This implies that we can think of $F$ as a pseudofunctor $\spadesuit_2\to\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}$.

Given a weight $W:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and pseudofunctor $G:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$ such that $\textup{colim}^W F$ exists, by lemma \ref{univnat}, we have a strong transformation $u:\textup{colim}^W \mathbb{B}(-,G) \to \mathbb{B}(-,\textup{colim}^W G):\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$. By precomposing with $F$ we then get a strong transformation $u_F:\textup{colim}^W \mathbb{B}(F-,G) \to \mathbb{B}(F-,\textup{colim}^W G):\spadesuit_2\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$.

Since $A$ is assumed to be atomic, $u_{FX}\,\simeq\, u_A$ is an equivalence. By lemma \ref{splitequiv}, this then implies that $u_{FY}\,\simeq\, u_B$ is an equivalence as well. This tells us that $\mathbb{B}(B,-):\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ preserves arbitrary colimits and thus $B$ is atomic as well.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{2retato}
Every atomic presheaf is a 2-retract of a representable presheaf.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
We can express $S$ as the colimit of $\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}:\mathbb{B}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ weighted by $S:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ with a strong transformation $\lambda:S\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-,S)$ given by the Yoneda lemma. Since $S$ is atomic we can now apply the functor $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,-)$ to this colimit and we have universal strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda_*:S\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-),\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,S))
\end{align*}
for the colimit of $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-):\mathbb{B} \to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ weighted by $S:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$. Since this is now a weighted colimit in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ we can explicitely define another colimit using theorem \ref{x1}. We get a universal strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\kappa: \, & S\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-),\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)) \\
\kappa_b(a): \, & \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\mathbb{B}(-,b))\to \textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-) \\
 & \kappa_b(a)(\alpha)=(a,\alpha)
\end{align*}
for the colimit in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$. Using theorem \ref{x2}, we can now form the colimit in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ by taking the idempotent completion. Let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the idempotent completion of $\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)$ with embedding $\iota:\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)\to \mathcal{K}$. We now have a colimit strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\kappa}:S\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-),\mathcal{K})
\end{align*}
given by $\widetilde{\kappa}=\iota_*\kappa$. Since both $\mathcal{K}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,S)$ are colimits of $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)$ weighted by $S$, we have an equivalence of categories $\Phi:\mathcal{K}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,S)$ such that $\Phi_*\widetilde{\kappa}\,\cong\, \lambda_*$. $\Phi$ is defined by the following: Let $(a,\alpha)$ with $a$ in $Sb$ and $\alpha:S\to\mathbb{B}(-,b)$ be an object in $\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)$. We now have
\begin{align*}
\Phi\iota(a,\alpha)=\lambda_b(a)\alpha:S\to S.
\end{align*}
This defines $\Phi$ up to isomorphism since by corollary \ref{kar1equ} for any category $\mathcal{C}$ and idempotent complete category $\mathcal{D}$, precomposition with $\iota_\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})$ defines an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\iota_\mathcal{C}^*:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{D})\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}).
\end{align*}
$\Phi$ now has the desired property since
\begin{align*}
(\Phi_*\widetilde{\kappa})_b(a)(\alpha)=\Phi\iota\kappa_b(a)(\alpha)=\Phi\iota(a,\alpha)=\lambda_b(a)\alpha=\left(\lambda_*\right)_b(a)(\alpha).
\end{align*}
We know that $\Phi$ has to be an equivalence, so there exists an object $k$ in $\mathcal{K}$ such that $\Phi k\,\cong\,\textup{id}_S$ via an isomorphism $\gamma:\Phi k \to\textup{id}_S$. Since $k$ lives in the idempotent completion of $\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)$, we know due to remark \ref{eobsplit} that there exists an object $(a,\alpha)$ and an idempotent $p:(a,\alpha)\to (a,\alpha)$ in $\textup{colim}^S \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})(S,\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_\mathbb{B}-)$ and morphisms $\widetilde{\varphi}:\iota(a,\alpha)\to k$ and $\widetilde{\psi}:k\to \iota(a,\alpha)$ in $\mathcal{K}$ such that $\widetilde{\varphi}\widetilde{\psi}=\textup{id}_k$ and $\widetilde{\psi}\widetilde{\varphi}=\iota(p)$. We now have
\begin{align*}
\varphi& =\gamma\Phi(\widetilde{\varphi}):\lambda_b(a)\alpha\to \textup{id}_S \text{ and} \\
\psi& =\Phi(\widetilde{\psi})\gamma{^{-1}}:\textup{id}_S\to \lambda_b(a)\alpha
\end{align*}
such that $\varphi\psi=\textup{id}_{\textup{id}_S}$. Therefore $S$ is a 2-idempotent splitting of the 2-idempotent $\alpha\lambda_b(a):\mathbb{B}(-,b)\to\mathbb{B}(-,b)$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{x8}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a locally idempotent complete category. The peudofunctor given by the composition
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B}) \arrow[r, "\textup{{\usefont{U}{dmjhira}{m}{n}\symbol{"48}}}_{\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})}"] & \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})) \arrow[r, "\iota_\mathbb{B}^*"] & \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
defines an equivalence of bicategories $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
First, we want to show that the pseudofunctor takes values in atomic objects, i.e., for every object $A_p$ in $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})$, the presheaf $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_p):\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is atomic. Remark \ref{x3} states that $A_p$ is a splitting of the 2-idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}$. By absoluteness of 2-splittings, we have that $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_p)$ is a splitting of an 2-idempotent on $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_{\textup{id}})=\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},\iota_\mathbb{B} A)$. Since $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is fully faithful, we have that $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},\iota_\mathbb{B} A)\,\simeq\,\mathbb{B}(-,A)$. This means that $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_p)$ is a retract of a representable presheaf and by lemma \ref{x7}, it therefore is atomic.

Next, we will show that the pseudofunctor is fully faithful. Since the Yoneda embedding is fully faithful and by theorem \ref{lscol} with $\mathbb{C}=\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$, precomposition with $\iota_\mathbb{B}$ is fully faithful, their composition must also be fully faithful.

Lastly, we check that the pseudofunctor is essentially surjective. Let $S$ be an atomic idempotent complete presheaf on $\mathbb{B}$. By proposition \ref{2retato}, there exists an object $A$ in $\mathbb{B}$ and a 2-idempotent $p$ on $A$ such that $S$ is a splitting of the 2-idempotent $p^*$ on $\mathbb{B}(-,A)$. Remark \ref{x3} states that $A_p$ is a splitting of the 2-idempotent $p$ on $A_{\textup{id}}=\iota_\mathbb{B} A$. By absoluteness of splittings $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_p)$ is a splitting of the 2-idempotent $p^*$ on $\textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},\iota_\mathbb{B} A)\,\simeq\, \mathbb{B}(-,A)$. Since splittings of 2-idempotents are unique up to equivalence, it follows that $S\,\simeq\, \textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})(\iota_\mathbb{B},A_p)$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{x10}
A locally idempotent complete bicategory is 2-idempotent complete if and only if it is complete under icAWCs.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a 2-idempotent complete bicategory. By proposition \ref{kar2emb} and theorem \ref{x8}, we now have $\mathbb{B}\,\simeq\, \textup{Kar}(\mathbb{B})\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$. Since $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}^\textup{at}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is complete under icAWCs, $\mathbb{B}$ must also be. The opposite direction follows analogously by proposition \ref{cau2emb}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
{(Adjoint Pseudofunctors)}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ be bicategories. Two pseu\-do\-functors $F:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$ and $G:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{B}$ are called \textit{adjoint} if there exist strong transformations $\eta:\textup{id}_\mathbb{B}\to GF$, $\epsilon:FG\to\textup{id}_\mathbb{C}$ and invertible modifications $\Gamma:\textup{id}_F \to (\epsilon F)\circ (F\eta)$ and $\Lambda:(G\epsilon)\circ (\eta G)\to \textup{id}_G$. We say that $F$ is \textit{left adjoint} to $G$, $G$ is \textit{right adjoint} to $F$ and the pseudofunctors $F$ and $G$ form an adjunction. We write $F\dashv G$.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{2adjequiv}
Adjoint functors induce an equivalence of categories
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{C}(Fb,c)\,\simeq\, \mathbb{B}(b,Gc)
\end{align*}
for each pair of objects $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$ and $c$ in $\mathbb{C}$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Let $f:Fb\to c$ be a 1-morphism in $\mathbb{B}$. We can define a morphism $f^\flat:b\to Gc$ via
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
b \arrow[r, "\eta_b"] & GFb \arrow[r, "Gf"] & Gc.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
Let $g:Fb\to c$ be another 1-morphism and $\theta:f\to g$ a 2-morphism. We can define a 2-morphism $\theta^\flat:f^\flat\to g^\flat$ via
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$b$};
\node at (2,0) {$GFb$};
\node at (5,0) {$Gc.$};
\node at (0.8,0.2) {$\eta_b$};
\node at (3.5,0.8) {$Gf$};
\node at (3.5,-0.8) {$Gg$};
\node at (3.7,0) {$G\theta$};
\draw[->] (0.25,0) to (1.4,0);
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (2.4,0.2) to (4.7,0.2);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (2.4,-0.2) to (4.7,-0.2);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (3.2,-0.3) to (3.2,0.3);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
One can check that this defines a functor $(-)^\flat:\mathbb{C}(Fb,c)\to \mathbb{B}(b,Gc)$. For a 1-morphism $f:b\to Gc$, we can analogously define a morphism $f^\sharp:Fb\to c$ via
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
Fb \arrow[r, "Ff"] & FGc \arrow[r, "\epsilon_C"] & c.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
This also defines a functor $(-)^\sharp:\mathbb{B}(b,Gc)\to \mathbb{C}(Fb,c)$. We will now show that these two functors form an equivalence of categories. We can construct a natural transformation $\textup{id}_{\mathbb{C}(Fb,c)} \to ((-)^\flat)^\sharp$ with components given by the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$Fb$};
\node at (3,0) {$FGFb$};
\node at (6,0) {$FGc$};
\node at (3,-3) {$Fb$};
\node at (6,-3) {$c,$};
\node at (1.5,0.3) {$F\eta_b$};
\node at (4.5,0.3) {$FGf$};
\node at (1.3,-1.7) {$\textup{id}_{Fb}$};
\node at (3.4,-1.5) {$\epsilon_{Fb}$};
\node at (6.3,-1.5) {$\epsilon_c$};
\node at (4.5,-3.3) {$f$};
\node at (1.9,-0.6) {$\Gamma_b$};
\node at (4.8,-1.7) {$\epsilon_f$};
\draw[->] (0.3,0) to (2.4,0);
\draw[->] (3.6,0) to (5.5,0);
\draw[->] (0.3,-0.2) to (2.7,-2.8);
\draw[->] (3,-0.2) to (3,-2.8);
\draw[->] (6,-0.2) to (6,-2.8);
\draw[->] (3.3,-3) to (5.8,-3);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.8,-1.2) to (2.5,-0.5);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (4.2,-1.8) to (5,-1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
i.e., we have an isomorphism $f\to (f^\flat)^\sharp$ given by
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
f \arrow[r, "r{^{-1}}"] & f\circ \textup{id}_{Fb} \arrow[r, "f\circ \Gamma_b"] & f\circ \epsilon_{Fb} \circ F\eta_B \arrow[r, "\epsilon_f\circ F\eta_b"] & \epsilon_C\circ FGf\circ F\eta_b=(f^\flat)^\sharp.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
That these isomorphism form a natural isomorphism, follows from the equality of the following two diagrams.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$Fb$};
\node at (3,0) {$FGFb$};
\node at (6,0) {$FGc$};
\node at (3,-3) {$Fb$};
\node at (6,-3) {$c$};
\node at (1.5,0.3) {$F\eta_b$};
\node at (4.5,0.7) {$FGg$};
\node at (1.3,-1.7) {$\textup{id}_{Fb}$};
\node at (3.4,-1.5) {$\epsilon_{Fb}$};
\node at (6.3,-1.5) {$\epsilon_c$};
\node at (4.5,-2.2) {$g$};
\node at (4.5,-3.8) {$f$};
\node at (1.9,-0.6) {$\Gamma_b$};
\node at (4.8,-1.2) {$\epsilon_f$};
\node at (4.65,-3) {$\theta$};
\draw[->] (0.3,0) to (2.4,0);
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (3.6,0.2) to (5.5,0.2);
\draw[->] (0.3,-0.2) to (2.7,-2.8);
\draw[->] (3,-0.2) to (3,-2.8);
\draw[->] (6,-0.2) to (6,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (3.3,-2.8) to (5.8,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (3.3,-3.2) to (5.8,-3.2);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.8,-1.2) to (2.5,-0.5);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (4.2,-1.3) to (5,-0.5);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (4.35,-3.3) to (4.35,-2.7);
\node at (7.5,-1.5) {$=$};
\node at (8,0) {$Fb$};
\node at (11,0) {$FGFb$};
\node at (14,0) {$FGc$};
\node at (11,-3) {$Fb$};
\node at (14,-3) {$c$};
\node at (9.5,0.3) {$F\eta_b$};
\node at (12.5,-0.7) {$FGf$};
\node at (12.5,0.7) {$FGg$};
\node at (9.3,-1.7) {$\textup{id}_{Fb}$};
\node at (11.4,-1.5) {$\epsilon_{Fb}$};
\node at (14.3,-1.5) {$\epsilon_c$};
\node at (12.5,-3.8) {$f$};
\node at (9.9,-0.6) {$\Gamma_b$};
\node at (12.8,-2.2) {$\epsilon_f$};
\node at (12.7,0) {$FG\theta$};
\draw[->] (8.3,0) to (10.4,0);
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (11.6,0.2) to (13.5,0.2);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (11.6,-0.2) to (13.5,-0.2);
\draw[->] (8.3,-0.2) to (10.7,-2.8);
\draw[->] (11,-0.2) to (11,-2.8);
\draw[->] (14,-0.2) to (14,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (11.3,-3.2) to (13.8,-3.2);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (9.8,-1.2) to (10.5,-0.5);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (12.2,-2.3) to (13,-1.5);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (12.15,-0.3) to (12.15,0.3);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
We thus have a natural isomorphism $\textup{id}_{\mathbb{C}(Fb,c)} \,\cong\, ((-)^\flat)^\sharp$ and analogously also a natural isomorphism $((-)^\sharp)^\flat\,\cong\, \textup{id}_{\mathbb{B}(b,Gc)}$. Therefore they form an equivalence of categories.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
\label{adjpres}
Left adjoint pseudofunctors preserve weighted colimits.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{J},\mathbb{B}$ be bicategories, $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ a weight, $F:\mathbb{J}\to\mathbb{B}$ pseudofunctor and $\lambda:W\to \mathbb{B}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F)$ a universal strong transformation. Now let $\mathbb{C}$ be another bicategory and $G:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{C}$ and $H:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{B}$ adjoint pseudofunctors with strong transformations $\eta:\textup{id}_\mathbb{B}\to HG$ and $\epsilon:GH\to \textup{id}_{\mathbb{C}}$. We will show that the strong transformation $G\lambda:W\to \mathbb{C}(GF-,G\textup{colim}^W F)$ is universal by showing that the following diagram commutes up to isomorphism for all objects $c$ in $\mathbb{C}$
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\mathbb{C}(G\textup{colim}^W F,c)} \arrow[r, "(G\lambda)^*"] \arrow[d, "(-)^\flat"] & {\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{J}^\textup{op},\textbf{\textup{Cat}})(W,\mathbb{C}(GF-,c))} \arrow[d, "(-)^\flat"] \\
{\mathbb{B}(\textup{colim}^W F,Hc)} \arrow[r, "\lambda^*"]                        & {\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{J}^\textup{op},\textbf{\textup{Cat}})(W,\mathbb{B}(F-,Hc))}                    
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
where $(-)^\flat$ is defined pointwise on strong transformation. All of the functors except $(G\lambda)^*$ are known to be equivalences of categories, so we only need to show that it commutes up to isomorphism. Let $f:G\textup{colim}^W F\to c$ be a 1-morphism in $\mathbb{C}$. We have an isomorphism $(f_*G\lambda)^\flat\,\cong\, f^\flat_*\lambda$ given by the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$Fj$};
\node at (4,0) {$\textup{colim}^W F$};
\node at (0,-3) {$HGFj$};
\node at (4,-3) {$HG\textup{colim}^W F$};
\node at (8,-3) {$Hc$};
\node at (2,0.3) {$\lambda_j(a)$};
\node at (0.35,-1.5) {$\eta_{Fj}$};
\node at (4.8,-1.5) {$\eta_{\textup{colim}^W F}$};
\node at (1.7,-3.3) {$HG\lambda_j(a)$};
\node at (6.3,-3.3) {$Hf$};
\node at (6.5,-1.3) {$f^\flat$};
\node at (2.5,-1.7) {$\eta_{\lambda_j(a)}$};
\draw[->] (0.3,0) to (3.1,0);
\draw[->] (0,-0.3) to (0,-2.75);
\draw[->] (4,-0.3) to (4,-2.75);
\draw[->] (0.7,-3) to (2.8,-3);
\draw[->] (4.8,-0.2) to (7.7,-2.8);
\draw[->] (5.25,-3) to (7.7,-3);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.5,-1.8) to (2.3,-1);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
where $j$ is an object in $\mathbb{J}$ and $a$ an object in $Wj$. We can also read off of this diagram that this isomorphism is natural. Thus $G$ preserves the weighted colimit.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- construction-1: body_md -->
\label{const}
Let $\mathbb{J}$ be a bicategory, $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ a weight and $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ a pseudofunctor. First we choose a set of objects $\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}$ for $\mathbb{J}$. We look at the diagram
\begin{center}
\vspace*{-\baselineskip}
\hspace*{-24pt}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\coprod_{j,j^\prime,j^{\prime\prime}\in\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj^{\prime\prime}\times \mathbb{J}(j^\prime,j^{\prime\prime})\times\mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\times Fj} \arrow[r, "d^0_2"{yshift=-2}, shift left=3] \arrow[r, "d^1_2"{yshift=-2}, shift left =-1] \arrow[r, "d^2_2"{yshift=-2}, shift left=-5] & {\coprod_{j,j^\prime\in\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj^\prime\times\mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\times Fj} \arrow[r, "d^0_1"{yshift=-2}, shift left=3] \arrow[r, "d^1_1"{yshift=-2}, shift left=-5] & \coprod_{j \in \textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj\times Fj \arrow[l, "s^0_0"'{yshift=-2}, shift left=1]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
where the maps are defined in the following way
\begin{align*}
d_2^0: & (a,g,f,x) \mapsto (a,g,F(f)x), \\
d_2^1: & (a,g,f,x) \mapsto (a,gf,x), \\
d_2^2: & (a,g,f,x) \mapsto (W(g)a,f,x), \\
d_1^0: & (a,f,x) \mapsto (a,F(f)x), \\
d_1^1: & (a,f,x) \mapsto (W(f)a,x), \\
s_0^0: & (a,x) \mapsto (a,\textup{id}_j,x).
\end{align*}

We now define the category $\textup{colim}^W F$ by taking the category $\coprod_{j \in \textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj\times Fj$ and freely adding isomorphism determined by $d^0_1$ and $d^1_1$ that are subject to relations given by $s^0_0$, $d^0_2$, $d^1_2$ and $d^2_2$.

For each pair of objects $j,j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$ and each object $(a,f,x)$ in $Wj^\prime\times\mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\times Fj$ we freely add an isomorphism 
\begin{align*}
\gamma_{a,f,x}: (a,F(f)x)\to (W(f)a,x)
\end{align*}
which assemble into a natural transformation
\begin{align*}
\gamma_{-,-,-}: (-,F(-)-) \to (W(-)-,-): Wj^\prime\times \mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime) \times Fj \to \textup{colim}^W F.
\end{align*}

These natural transformations have to satisfy the following two conditions. For all $j,j^\prime,j^{\prime\prime}\in\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}$, $x$ in $Fj$, $f:j\to j^\prime$, $g:j^\prime\to j^{\prime\prime}$ and $a$ in $Wj^{\prime\prime}$, the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{(a,F(g)F(f)x)} \arrow[d, "{(\textup{id}_a,F^2\textup{id}_x)}"] \arrow[r, "{\gamma_{a,g,F(f)x}}"] & {(W(g)a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{\gamma_{W(g)a,f,x}}"] & {(W(f)W(g)a,x)} \arrow[d, "{(W^2\textup{id}_a,\textup{id}_x)}"] \\
{(a,F(gf)x)} \arrow[rr, "{\gamma_{a,gf,x}}"]                               &                                                   & {(W(gf)a,x)}                            
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
has to commute, and for all $j\in\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}$, $x$ in $Fj$ and $a$ in $Wj$, the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{(a,\textup{id}_{Fj}x)} \arrow[r, "="] \arrow[d, "{(\textup{id}_a,F^0\textup{id}_x)}"] & {(a,x)} \arrow[r, "="] & {(\textup{id}_{Wj}a,x)} \arrow[d, "{(W^0\textup{id}_a,\textup{id}_x)}"] \\
{(a,F(\textup{id}_j)x)} \arrow[rr, "{\gamma_{a,\textup{id}_j,x}}"]      &                        & {(W(\textup{id}_j)a,x)}                         
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
has to commute. $F^2$ and $F^0$ denote the coherence data of the pseudofunctor $F$ and analogously for $W$. We call these two diagrams the naturality and unitality conditions of $\gamma$. $\textup{colim}^W F$ is now the category obtained by adding these ismorphism subject to the given relations freely to $\coprod_{j \in \textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj\times Fj$. We now also define the functors
\begin{align*}
\gamma_j:W(j)\times F(j) \to \textup{colim}^W F
\end{align*}
which are given by inclusions since $W(j)\times F(j)$ is a subcategory of $\textup{colim}^W F$.

We can now define a strong transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda:W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F):\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}.
\end{align*}
For each object $j$ in $\mathbb{J}$, we have a 1-morphism $\lambda_j:Wj\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Fj,\textup{colim}^W F)$ given by $\lambda_j(a)(x)=\gamma_j(a,x)=(a,x)$
for each $a$ in $Wj$ and $x$ in $Fj$. Since $\gamma_j$ is a functor, both $\lambda_j$ and $\lambda_j(a)$ also define functors.

For each pair of objects $j,j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$, we also have a natural transformation
\begin{align*}
\lambda: \lambda_{j^\prime}^*\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F)\to (\lambda_j)_*W:\mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Wj^\prime,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Fj,\textup{colim}^W F))
\end{align*}
with component morphisms  $\lambda_f: F(f)^*\lambda_{j^\prime} \to \lambda_j W(f)$ which are defined by
\begin{align*}
\lambda_{f,a,x} =\gamma_{a,f,x}: \left(F(f)^*\lambda_{j^\prime}(a)\right)(x) & = \lambda_{j^\prime}(a)(F(f)x) = (a,F(f)x) \\
& \to (W(f)a,x)=\lambda_j(W(f)a)(x)
\end{align*}
for each $a$ in $Wj^\prime$ and $x$ in $Fj$. The naturality of $\lambda$ and $\lambda_f$ and $\lambda_{f,a}$ all follow from the naturality of $\gamma$. Lastly we need to check that $\lambda$ satisfies the naturality and unitality conditions, this follows since $\gamma$ needs to satisfy its own naturality and unitality conditions.
<!-- end construction-1 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{x1}
Given a bicategory $\mathbb{J}$, a weight $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ and a pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$, construction \ref{const} defines a colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We next need to check that precomposition with $\lambda: W \to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F)$ defines an equivalence of pseudofunctors
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{colim}^W F,-)\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F,-)).
\end{align*}
For this it suffices to check that it defines an equivalence of categories
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{colim}^W F,\mathcal{C})\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C}))
\end{align*}
for each category $\mathcal{C}$. As it turns out, a functor $\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$ is determined by the same data as a strong transformation $W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ just presented in different ways. This will lead to an isomorphism of categories.

A strong transformation $\epsilon:W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ is given by a $\mathbb{J}$-indexed family of functors $\epsilon_j:Wj\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Fj,\mathcal{C})$ and for each morphism $f:j\to j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$ a natural isomorphism $\epsilon_f:F(f)^*\epsilon_{j^\prime}\to\epsilon_j W(f):Wj^\prime\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Fj,\mathcal{C})$ such that the $\epsilon_f$ are natural in $f$ and satisfy the naturality and unitality conditions.

Using the fact that for categories $\mathcal{C}_1,\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{D}$ we have an isomorphism of categories
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C}_1\times\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{D})\,\cong\,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C}_1,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C}_2,\mathcal{D}))
\end{align*} 
given by currying, know that the family $(\epsilon_j)_{j\in\textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}$ is equivalent to a $\mathbb{J}$-indexed family of functors $\widetilde{\epsilon}_j:Wj\times Fj\to \mathcal{C}$ and the $\epsilon_f$ turn into natural transformations 
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\epsilon}_f:\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^\prime}(-,F(f)-)\to \widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W(f)-,-):Wj^\prime\times Fj\to\mathcal{C}
\end{align*}
Naturality in $f$ now means that they assemble into a natural transformation
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\epsilon}:\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^\prime}(-,F(-)-)\to \widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W(-)-,-):Wj^\prime\times \mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\times Fj\to\mathcal{C}.
\end{align*}
The naturality condition tranlates into the following commutative diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^{\prime\prime}}(a,F(g)F(f)x)} \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^{\prime\prime}}(\textup{id}_a,F^2\textup{id}_x)}"] \arrow[r, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{a,g,F(f)x}}"] & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^\prime}(W(g)a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{W(g)a,f,x}}"] & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W(f)W(g)a,x)} \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W^2\textup{id}_a,\textup{id}_x)}"] \\
{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^{\prime\prime}}(a,F(gf)x)} \arrow[rr, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{a,gf,x}}"]                               &                                                   & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W(gf)a,x)}                            
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
which has to hold for all objects $j,j^\prime,j^{\prime\prime}$ in $\mathbb{J}$, morphisms $f:j\to j^\prime$ and $g:j^\prime\to j^{\prime\prime}$ and objects $a$ in $Wj^{\prime\prime}$ and $x$ in $Fj$. The unitality condition tranlates into the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(a,\textup{id}_{Fj}x)} \arrow[r, "="] \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(\textup{id}_a,F^0\textup{id}_x)}"] & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(a,x)} \arrow[r, "="] & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(\textup{id}_{Wj}a,x)} \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W^0\textup{id}_a,\textup{id}_x)}"] \\
{\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(a,F(\textup{id}_j)x)} \arrow[rr, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{a,\textup{id}_j,x}}"]      &                        & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_j(W(\textup{id}_j)a,x)}                         
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
which has to commute for all objects $j$ in $\mathbb{J}$, $a$ in $Wj$ and $x$ in $Fj$. We can already see that these are exactly the conditions we asked of $\gamma$ when constructing $\textup{colim}^W F$. We will now look at the data that a functor $G:\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$ consists of. Since $\textup{colim}^W F$ was constructed by adding isomorphisms to the category $\coprod_{j \in \textup{Ob}\mathbb{J}}Wj\times Fj$, the functor $G$ consists a family of functors $G_j:Wj\times Fj\to \mathcal{C}$ that also has to map the components $\gamma$ on isomorphisms in $\mathcal{C}$ that have to satisfy the same properties as $\gamma$. So we have a natural transformation 
\begin{align*}
G(\gamma_{-,-,-}):G(-,F(-)-)\to G(W(-)-,-):Wj^\prime\times \mathbb{J}(j,j^\prime)\times Fj\to\mathcal{C}
\end{align*}
and the components of this natural transformation also have to satisfy the unitality and naturality conditions. So we indeed see that a functor $\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$ consists of the same data as a strong transformation $W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ and the presentation of this data only differs by currying. This currying is also induced by precomposition with $\lambda$ since given a functor $G:\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$, the strong transformation $G_*\lambda:W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ is defined by
\begin{align*}
(G_*\lambda)_j(a)(x)=(G_*\lambda_j)(a)(x)=(G\lambda_j(a))(x)=G(\lambda_j(a)(x))=G(a,x)
\end{align*}
for objects $j$ in $\mathbb{J}$, $a$ in $Wj$ and $x$ in $Fj$, and by
\begin{align*}
(G_*\lambda)_{f,a,x}=G\lambda_{f,a,x}=G\gamma_{a,f,x}
\end{align*}
for objects $j,j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$, a morphism $f:j\to j^\prime$ and objects $a$ in $Wj^\prime$ and $x$ in $Fj$. To show that this induces an isomorphism of categories
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{colim}^W F,\mathcal{C})\,\cong\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C}))
\end{align*}
we also have to show that a natural transformation between such functors also only differs by currying from a modification between such strong transformations. Let $\epsilon,\eta:W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ be two strong transformations and let $\Gamma:\epsilon\to\eta$ be a modification between them. $\Gamma$ consists of a $\mathbb{J}$-indexed family of natural transformations
\begin{align*}
\Gamma_j:\epsilon_j\to\eta_j:Wj\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(Fj,\mathcal{C})
\end{align*}
which since $\Gamma$ is a modification has to satisfy a certain property. Using currying, this the natural transformations $\Gamma_j$ correspond to natural transformations
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{\Gamma}_j:\widetilde{\epsilon}\to\widetilde{\eta}:Wj\times Fj\to \mathcal{C}
\end{align*}
and the property they need to satisfy can be written as the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j^\prime}(a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{\widetilde{\epsilon}_{a,f,x}}"] \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\Gamma}_{j^\prime,a,F(f)x}}"] & {\widetilde{\epsilon}_{j}(W(f)a,x)} \arrow[d, "{\widetilde{\Gamma}_{j,W(f)a,x}}"] \\
{\widetilde{\eta}_{j^\prime}(a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{\widetilde{\eta}_{a,f,x}}"]                                                     & {\widetilde{\eta}_{j}(W(f)a,x)}                                              
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
which has to commute for all objects $j,j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$, morphisms $f:j\to j^\prime$ and objects $a$ in $Wj^\prime$ and $x$ in $Fj$. Now let $G,H:\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$ be two functors and let $\varphi:G\to H$ be a natural transformations. We've already seen that due to the structure of $\textup{colim}^W F$ the two functors $G,H$ consists of $\mathbb{J}$-indexed families of functors $G_j,H_j:Wj\times Fj\to \mathcal{C}$ together with the natural transformations $G(\gamma)$ and $H(\gamma)$. A natural transformation $\varphi:G\to H$ now consist of a $\mathbb{J}$-indexed family of natural transformations $\varphi_j:G_j\to H_j$ which also have to be natural with respect to $\gamma$. This can be represented by the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
{G_{j^\prime}(a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{G(\gamma_{a,f,x})}"] \arrow[d, "{\varphi_{j^\prime,(a,F(f)x)}}"] & {G_{j}(W(f)a,x)} \arrow[d, "{\varphi_{j,(W(f)a,x)}}"] \\
{H_{j^\prime}(a,F(f)x)} \arrow[r, "{H(\gamma_{a,f,x})}"]                                     & {H_{j}(W(f)a,x)}                                  
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
which has to commute for all objects $j,j^\prime$ in $\mathbb{J}$, morphisms $f:j\to j^\prime$ and objects $a$ in $Wj^\prime$ and $x$ in $Fj$. So now we also see that a natural transformation $\varphi:G\to H$ between functors $G,H:\textup{colim}^W F\to \mathcal{C}$ consists of the same data as a modification $\Gamma:\epsilon\to\eta$ between strong transformations $\epsilon,\eta:W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ and the presentation of this data also only differs by currying.

Thus, we have shown that precomposition with $\lambda:W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\textup{colim}^W F)$, which does the same as currying, actually defines an isomorphism
\begin{align*}
\lambda^*:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\textup{colim}^W F,\mathcal{C})\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})).
\end{align*}
for each category $\mathcal{C}$. Thus $\textup{colim}^W F$ together with $\lambda$ forms a colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{catcc}
The 2-category $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ of categories is cocomplete, i.e., for every bicategory $\mathbb{J}$, every weight $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ and every pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ exists.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{PshCocomp}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory. The bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})$ is cocomplete.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{J}$ be a bicategory, $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ a weight and $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})$ a pseudofunctor. We can construct a colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ in the following way. Let $A$ be an object in $\mathbb{B}$. We now have the pseudofunctor $F(-)(A):\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ and since $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ is cocomplete the colimit of $F(-)(A)$ weighted by $W$ exists, i.e., we have a universal strong transformation $\lambda_A:W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F(-)(A),\textup{colim}^W F(-)(A))$.

We now define the presheaf $\textup{colim}^W F:\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ via $\textup{colim}^W F(A)=\textup{colim}^W F(-)(A)$. Let $B$ be another object in $\mathbb{B}$ and $f:A\to B$ a morphism. We can now define the strong transformation $F(-)(f)^*\lambda_A:W\to \textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F(-)(B),\textup{colim}^W F(A))$ which has components $(F(-)(f)^*\lambda_A)_j(a)=\lambda_{A,j}(a)F(j)(f)$
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
F(j)(B) \arrow[r, "F(j)(f)"] & F(j)(A) \arrow[r, "{\lambda_{A,j}(a)}"] & \textup{colim}^W F(A)
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
for each $j$ in $\mathbb{J}$ and $a$ in $Wj$. By the universal property of the colimit, we get a morphism 
\begin{align*}
\textup{colim}^W F(f):\textup{colim}^W F(B)\to\textup{colim}^W F(A)
\end{align*}
and an isomorphism $\lambda_f:\textup{colim}^W F(f)_*\lambda_B \to F(-)(f)^*\lambda_A$ which we can represent by the following diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
F(j)(B) \arrow[r, "F(j)(f)"] \arrow[d, "{\lambda_{B,j}(a)}"']                        & F(j)(A) \arrow[d, "{\lambda_{A,j}(a)}"] \\
\textup{colim}^W F(B) \arrow[r, "\textup{colim}^WF(f)"'] \arrow[ru, "{\lambda_{f,j,a}}", Rightarrow] & \textup{colim}^W F(A)                          
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
For a second 1-morphism $g:A\to B$ and a 2-morphism $\theta:f\to g$, we get a morphism of strong transformations
\begin{align*}
F(-)(\theta)^*\lambda_A:F(-)(f)^*\lambda_A\to F(-)(g)^*\lambda_A
\end{align*}
which gives us a morphism $\textup{colim}^W F(\theta):\textup{colim}^W F(f)\to \textup{colim}^W F(g)$. This can be represented as
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$F(j)(B)$};
\node at (4,0) {$F(j)(A)$};
\node at (0,-3) {$\textup{colim}^W F(B)$};
\node at (4,-3) {$\textup{colim}^W F(A)$};
\node at (2,1.1) {$F(j)(g)$};
\node at (2,-1.1) {$F(j)(f)$};
\node at (2,-4) {$\textup{colim}^W F(f)$};
\node at (-0.7,-1.5) {$\lambda_{B,j}(a)$};
\node at (4.7,-1.5) {$\lambda_{A,j}(a)$};
\node at (2.2,0) {$F(j)(\theta)$};
\node at (1.4,-1.8) {$\lambda_{f,j,a}$};
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (0.25,0.25) to (3.75,0.25);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (0.25,-0.25) to (3.75,-0.25);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (0.5,-3.25) to (3.5,-3.25);
\draw[->] (0,-0.3) to (0,-2.7);
\draw[->] (4,-0.3) to (4,-2.7);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.3,-0.3) to (1.3,0.3);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.3,-2.5) to (2.7,-1.7);
\node at (6,-1.5) {$=$};
\node at (8,0) {$F(j)(B)$};
\node at (12,0) {$F(j)(A)$};
\node at (8,-3) {$\textup{colim}^W F(B)$};
\node at (12,-3) {$\textup{colim}^W F(A)$};
\node at (10,1) {$F(j)(g)$};
\node at (10,-2) {$\textup{colim}^W F(g)$};
\node at (10,-4) {$\textup{colim}^W F(f)$};
\node at (7.3,-1.5) {$\lambda_{B,j}(a)$};
\node at (12.7,-1.5) {$\lambda_{A,j}(a)$};
\node at (10.1,-3) {\tiny{$\textup{colim}^W F(\theta)$}};
\node at (9.4,-0.6) {$\lambda_{g,j,a}$};
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (8.25,0.25) to (11.75,0.25);
\draw[->, out=30, in=150] (8.5,-2.75) to (11.5,-2.75);
\draw[->, out=-30, in=-150] (8.5,-3.25) to (11.5,-3.25);
\draw[->] (8,-0.3) to (8,-2.7);
\draw[->] (12,-0.3) to (12,-2.7);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (9.25,-3.4) to (9.25,-2.6);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (9.3,-1.3) to (10.7,-0.5);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
The presheaf $\textup{colim}^W F$ is now well defined along with a strong transformation $\lambda:W\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})(F,\textup{colim}^W F)$ with components $\lambda_{j,A}(a)=\lambda_{A,j}(a)$. We must now show that $\lambda$ defines a universal strong transformation. Let $\kappa:W\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})(F,S)$ be another strong transformation for a presheaf $S$. For an object $A$ in $\mathbb{B}$, we can then define the natural transformation $\kappa_A:\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{B})(F(-)(A),S(A))$ and by the universal property of the colimit, we get a morphism $\varphi_A:\textup{colim}^W F(A)\to S(A)$ such that $\kappa_A\,\cong\, (\varphi_A)_*\lambda_A$. The $\varphi_A$ assemble into a morphism of presheafs $\varphi:\textup{colim}^W F\to S$ and we get an isomorphism $\kappa\,\cong\, \varphi_*\lambda$. This shows that $\lambda$ defines a colimit.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
For a category $\mathcal{C}$ and a idempotent complete category $\mathcal{D}$, the category $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})$ of functors and natural transformations is idempotent complete.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Let $F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}$ be a functor and $p:F\to F$ an idempotent natural transformation, i.e., for every object $c$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the morphism $p_c:Fc\to Fc$ is an idempotent. Since these are morphisms in $\mathcal{D}$, we can choose a splitting for every idempotent $p_c$. We now choose for every $c$ in $\mathcal{C}$ an object $Sc$ in $\mathcal{D}$ and morphisms $f_c:Fc\to Sc$ and $g_c:Sc\to Fc$ such that $g_c f_c=p_c$ and $f_c g_c=\textup{id}_{Sc}$. We can now turn $S$ into a functor. Let $h:c\to d$ be a morphism in $\mathcal{C}$. We define $S(h)=f_d F(h) g_c$. We now have $S(\textup{id}_c)=f_c F(\textup{id}_c) g_c=f_c g_c=\textup{id}_{Sc}$ and for another morphism $k:d\to e$, we have
\begin{align*}
S(k) S(h) & \, =f_e F(k) g_d f_d F(h) g_c=f_e F(k) p_d F(h) g_c=f_e F(k) F(h) p_c g_c \\
& = f_e F(kh) g_c f_c g_c= f_e F(kh) g_c \textup{id}_{Sc} = S(kh)
\end{align*}
which shows that $S$ defines a functor. We lastly need to show that the $f_c$ and $g_c$ define natural transformations $f:F\to S$ and $g:S \to F$. For this we need to check that the following two diagrams commute.
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
Fc \arrow[r, "F(h)"] \arrow[d, "f_c"] & Fd \arrow[d, "f_d"] & Sc \arrow[r, "S(h)"] \arrow[d, "g_c"] & Sd \arrow[d, "g_d"] \\
Sc \arrow[r, "S(h)"]                  & Sd                  & Fc \arrow[r, "F(h)"]                  & Fd                 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
We can show
\begin{align*}
S(h) f_c = f_d F(h) g_c f_c=f_d F(h) p_c = f_d p_d F(h) = f_d g_d f_d F(h)= \textup{id}_{Sd} f_d F(h) = f_d F(h) 
\end{align*}
and thus $f:F\to S$ defines a natural transformation and
\begin{align*}
g_d S(h) = g_d f_d F(h)g_c = p_d F(h) g_c = F(h) p_c g_c = F(h) g_c f_c g_c = F(h) g_c \textup{id}_{Sc} = F(h) g_c
\end{align*}
and thus $g:S\to F$ defines a natural transformation. The natural transformations $f$ and $g$ now satisfy $gf=p$ and $fg=\textup{id}_{S}$ and thus $p$ splits.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{Catlic}
The bicategories $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ are locally idempotent complete.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{x2}
The locally idempotent complete bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ of idempotent complete categories is ic-cocomplete, i.e., for every bicategory $\mathbb{J}$, every ic-weight $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and every pseudofunctor $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ the colimit of $F$ weighted by $W$ exists.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Let $\mathbb{J}$ be a bicategory, $W:\mathbb{J}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ a weight and $F:\mathbb{J}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ a pseudofunctor. We can regard both $W$ and $F$ as pseudofunctors taking values in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$. By theorem \ref{x1}, we now know that we can construct a category $\mathcal{C}$ along with a strong transformation $\lambda:W\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F-,\mathcal{C})$ such that we have a natural equivalence
\begin{align*}
\lambda^* :\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(\mathcal{C},-)\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}(F,-)).
\end{align*}
We know by theorem \ref{1adj}, that we have a left adjoint pseudofunctor $\textup{Kar}:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ and thus, by proposition \ref{adjpres}, we have a natural equivalence
\begin{align*}
(\textup{Kar}\lambda)^*:\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}),-)\to\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textup{Kar} F,-))
\end{align*}
where $\textup{Kar}\lambda$ is defined by
\begin{align*}
(\textup{Kar}\lambda)_j(a)=\textup{Kar}(\lambda_j(a)):\textup{Kar}(Fj)\to\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})
\end{align*}
for each $j$ in $\mathbb{J}$ and $a$ in $Wj$. Since $F$ already takes values in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$, $F$ and $\textup{Kar} F$ are equivalent with an equivalence given by $\iota_F:F\to \textup{Kar} F$ which has components given by $\iota_{Fj}:Fj\to \textup{Kar}(Fj)$. We also know that the diagram
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzcd}
Fj \arrow[d, "\iota_{Fj}"] \arrow[r, "\lambda_j(a)"] & \mathcal{C} \arrow[d, "\iota_\mathcal{C}"] \\
\textup{Kar}(Fj) \arrow[r, "\textup{Kar}(\lambda_j(a))"]             & \textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C})                 
\end{tikzcd}
\end{center}
commutes. These two facts combined tell us that we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
((\iota_\mathcal{C})_*\lambda)^*: \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}),-)\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(F,-))
\end{align*}
and since $W$ takes values in $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}^\textup{op}$ and $\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}$ is locally idempotent complete, we get the desired result that we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
((\iota_\mathcal{C})_*\lambda)^*: \textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(\textup{Kar}(\mathcal{C}),-)\to \textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{J})(W,\textbf{\textup{Cat}}_\textup{ic}(F,-))
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
For a bicategory $\mathbb{B}$ and a locally idempotent complete bicategory $\mathbb{C}$ the bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Bicat}}(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{C})$ is locally idempotent complete.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Let $F,G:\mathbb{B}\to \mathbb{C}$ be pseudofuncors, $\alpha:F\to G$ a strong transformation and $p:\alpha\to \alpha$ an idempotent modification, i.e., for each object $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$ the morphism $p_b:\alpha_b\to \alpha_b$ in $\mathbb{C}(Fb,Gb)$ is idempotent. Since $\mathbb{C}$ is locally idempotent complete, we can choose a splitting for each $p_b$ for all $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$. We therefore have 1-morphisms $s_b:Fb\to Gb$, and 2-morphisms $f_b:\alpha_b\to s_b$ and $g_b:s_b\to \alpha_b$ such that $g_b f_b=p_b$ and $f_b g_b=\textup{id}_{s_b}$. $s:F\to G$ forms a strong transformation with component 2-morphisms $s_h:G(h)s_b\to s_c F(h)$ given by
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node at (0,0) {$Fb$};
\node at (3,0) {$Fc$};
\node at (0,-3) {$Gb$};
\node at (3,-3) {$Gc$};
\node at (1.5,0.25) {$F(h)$};
\node at (1.5,-3.25) {$G(h)$};
\node at (-0.85,-1.5) {$s_b$};
\node at (0.8,-1) {$\alpha_b$};
\node at (2.2,-2) {$\alpha_c$};
\node at (3.85,-1.5) {$s_c$};
\node at (0,-1.4) {$g_b$};
\node at (3,-1.4) {$f_b$};
\node at (1.35,-1.4) {$\alpha_h$};
\draw[->] (0.3,0) to (2.7,0);
\draw[->] (0.3,-3) to (2.7,-3);
\draw[->, out=-120, in=120] (-0.2,-0.2) to (-0.2,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=-60, in=60] (0.2,-0.2) to (0.2,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=-120, in=120] (2.8,-0.2) to (2.8,-2.8);
\draw[->, out=-60, in=60] (3.2,-0.2) to (3.2,-2.8);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (-0.4,-1.8) to (0.4,-1.8);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (2.6,-1.8) to (3.4,-1.8);
\draw[-implies, double equal sign distance] (1.3,-2.2) to (2.1,-0.8);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
for a 1-morphism $h:b\to c$ in $\mathbb{B}$. $f:\alpha\to s$ and $g:s\to \alpha$ now form modifications such that $gf=p$ and $fg=\textup{id}_s$ and thus $p$ splits.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{Pshlic}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory. The bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ of idempotent complete presheaves on $\mathbb{B}$ is locally idempotent complete.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{Pshicc}
Let $\mathbb{B}$ be a bicategory. The locally idempotent complete bicategory $\textbf{\textup{Psh}}_\textup{ic}(\mathbb{B})$ is ic-cocomplete.
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
{(Extensions)}
Let $\mathbb{B}$, $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{D}$ be bicategories, $F:\mathbb{B}\to \mathbb{C}$ an arbitrary pseudofunctor and $\iota:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{D}$ a fully faithful pseudofunctor. An \textit{extension} of $F$ along $\iota$ is a pseudofunctor $F^\prime:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ together with an equivalence of pseudofunctors $\varphi:F^\prime\iota\to F$.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{ext}
Let $\mathbb{B}$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{D}$, $F:\mathbb{B}\to \mathbb{C}$  and $\iota:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{D}$ be as above. An extension of $F$ along $\iota$ exists, if for all $d\in\mathbb{D}$ the colimit of $F$ weighted by $\mathbb{D}(\iota-,d):\mathbb{B}^\textup{op}\to\textbf{\textup{Cat}}$ exists.
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
We define $F^\prime$ on objects $d\in\mathbb{D}$ to be the weighted colimit $\textup{colim}^{\mathbb{D}(\iota-,d)}F$. On Hom-categories, we have functors $\mathbb{D}(d,d^\prime) \to \mathbb{C}(F^\prime d,F^\prime d^\prime)$ which are defined in the following way:

For every 1-morphism $f:d\to d^\prime$, we have a strong transformation $f_*:\mathbb{D}(\iota-,d)\to \mathbb{D}(\iota-,d^\prime)$ given by postcompostion. By our assumption, we have a universal strong transformation $\lambda^d:\mathbb{D}(\iota-,d)\to\mathbb{C}(F-,F^\prime d)$ for each $d\in\mathbb{D}$. We can now form $\lambda^{d^\prime}\circ f_*: \mathbb{D}(\iota-,d)\to\mathbb{C}(F-,F^\prime d^\prime)$.

For all $d\in \mathbb{D}$ we have an equivalence of categories
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{C}(F^\prime d, c)\,\simeq\, \textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(\mathbb{D}(\iota-,d),\mathbb{C}(F-,c))
\end{align*}
given by precomposition with $\lambda^d$. We define $\eta^d$ to be an inverse to this equivalence and can now define the functors $F^\prime:\mathbb{D}(d,d^\prime) \to \mathbb{C}(F^\prime d,F^\prime d^\prime)$ via $F^\prime f =\eta^d(\lambda^{d^\prime}\circ f_*)$.

We now need to check that this assignment is functorial, i.e., that for objects $d$, $d^\prime$, $d^{\prime\prime}$ and morphisms $f:d\to d^\prime$ and $g:d^\prime \to d^{\prime\prime}$,  we have coherence isomorphisms $\textup{id}_{F^\prime d}\,\cong\, F^\prime \textup{id}_d$ and $F^\prime g \circ F^\prime f \,\cong\, F^\prime(g\circ f)$ subject to compatibility conditions.

The first isomorphism is simply given by $F^\prime \textup{id}_d = \eta^d(\lambda^d \circ (\textup{id}_d)_*) \,\cong\, \eta^d(\lambda^d)\,\cong\, \textup{id}_{F^\prime d}$. For the second one, we need to find an isomorphism
\begin{align*}
F^\prime g\circ F^\prime f=\eta^{d^\prime}(\lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ g_*)\circ \eta^d(\lambda^{d^\prime} \circ f_*)\,\cong\, \eta^d(\lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ(g\circ f)_*)=F^\prime(g\circ f). 
\end{align*}
By precomposing both sides with $\lambda^d$, we have a chain of isomorphisms
\begin{align*}
F^\prime g\circ F^\prime f \circ \lambda^d & = \eta^{d^\prime}(\lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ g_*)\circ \eta^d(\lambda^{d^\prime} \circ f_*)\circ \lambda^d \,\cong\, \eta^{d^\prime}(\lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ g_*)\circ \lambda^{d^\prime} \circ f_* \\
& \,\cong\, \lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ g_* \circ f_* \,\cong\, \eta^d(\lambda^{d^{\prime\prime}}\circ(g\circ f)_*) \circ \lambda^d = F^\prime(g\circ f) \circ \lambda_d.
\end{align*}
Since precomposing with $\lambda^d$ is an equivalence, we have our desired isomorphism. It is a relatively straightforward calculation to check that these isomorphism satisfy compatibility with associators and unitors and therefore define a pseudofunctor.

Finally we need to show that $F^\prime$ actually extends $F$, i.e., that we have an equivalence $F^\prime\iota \,\simeq\, F$. This equivalence exists because of the Yoneda lemma as we will elaborate briefly.

For an object $b$ in $\mathbb{B}$, $F^\prime \iota b$ is defined by taking the colimit of $F$ weighted by $\mathbb{D}(\iota-,\iota b)$. But since $\iota$ is fully faithful, this weight is equivalent to the representable weight $\mathbb{B}(-,b)$ and by the Yoneda lemma we have an equivalence
\begin{align*}
\textbf{\textup{Psh}}(\mathbb{J})(\mathbb{B}(-,b),\mathbb{C}(F-,c))\,\simeq\, \mathbb{C}(Fb,c)
\end{align*}
for all objects $c$ in $\mathbb{C}$. Thus the colimit of $F$ weighted by $\mathbb{D}(\iota-,\iota b)$ is equivalent to $Fb$, giving us our desired equivalence.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
The extension constructed here is a special case of a bicategorical left Kan extension.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
